#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Long-term Incentive Plan (LTIP)
Performance and recognition become most powerful when individual success is directly linked to organizational success. 
Tanla’s Long-Term Incentive Plan (LTIP) is designed to strengthen this connection by transforming employees into true co-
owners of the business. Through performance-based RSU grants, the plan shifts the employee mindset from managing short-
term responsibilities to creating long-term enterprise value, reinforcing accountability, retention, and long-term alignment.
LTIP coverage expanded from 5% of the workforce in FY25 to 7% in FY26 as the organization broadened participation to 
include a larger pool of key employees responsible for delivering Tanla’s long-term growth ambitions. The expansion reflects 
a deliberate strategy to align high-impact talent with enterprise-level goals that extend beyond individual KRAs. By linking 
rewards to the achievement of ambitious organizational targets, LTIP encourages employees to think beyond their immediate 
responsibilities, collaborate across functions, and contribute to outcomes that accelerate the company’s next phase of 
growth. In doing so, the program strengthens a culture of ownership, where employees are motivated not only by incentives, 
but by the opportunity to directly shape and participate in Tanla’s long-term success.
Excellence as a Way of Working
Recognition at Tanla extends beyond titles, designations, and compensation. Through initiatives such as CEO Connect 
sessions with high performers across the Group, employees receive direct visibility to leadership and an opportunity to 
engage in meaningful conversations about their aspirations, contributions, and future potential. These moments of personal 
acknowledgement complement formal rewards by reinforcing a simple but powerful message: exceptional performance is it 
is seen, valued, and celebrated.
Ultimately, excellence is sustained by an ecosystem that continuously develops people, recognises contribution, and 
reinforces ownership at every stage of the employee journey. By integrating capability building, performance, engagement, 
and recognition into a single system, Tanla is creating an organisation where excellence is a discipline that compounds over 
time.
04 | Ownership
Ownership is most powerful when it comes from within. It cannot be imposed through policies or processes; it is cultivated 
through trust, empowerment, and a shared sense of purpose. When people feel connected to the organisation’s success and 
confident that they will be supported along the way, they take greater responsibility for outcomes and contribute beyond the 
boundaries of their roles.
This sense of ownership is rooted in a reciprocal relationship. Employees bring their skills, commitment, and ambition to work 
every day; in return, the organisation provides opportunities for growth, equitable treatment, safe working conditions, and 
mechanisms that safeguard wellbeing and employee rights. Together, these create the trust that enables individuals and 
teams to perform at their best while building the confidence to innovate, collaborate, and create long-term value.
Talent Retention: The Compound Return on People Investment
Voluntary turnover at Tanla declined to 17.1% in FY26, the lowest level recorded in four years. The improvement reflects 
the cumulative impact of sustained investments in employee experience, career development, workplace flexibility, and 
leadership engagement.
Over the past three years, the organisation has focused on understanding and addressing the underlying drivers of employee 
turnover rather than simply managing its outcomes. As a result, retention improved across age groups, management levels, 
and gender cohorts, strengthening organisational stability and preserving critical institutional knowledge.
For a technology organisation where expertise compounds over time, retaining experienced talent is as important as attracting 
new capability. Lower turnover helps preserve customer relationships, sustain technical depth, accelerate execution, and 
strengthen leadership continuity across the business.

Supporting Employees Through Life Stages
Retention is ultimately a reflection of how employees experience the organisation during moments that matter most.
During FY26, Tanla continued to strengthen support mechanisms for employees navigating significant personal and 
professional transitions, including maternity, medical situations, caregiving responsibilities, and extended leave requirements. 
Flexible work arrangements, personalised support, and manager engagement helped employees remain connected to the 
organisation while balancing personal commitments.
Deliberate focus was placed on supporting women employees returning from maternity leave and employees transitioning 
back from extended absences for special reasons, ensuring they could re-engage confidently with meaningful work, career 
progression opportunities, and leadership support.
The result was a significant reduction in women’s voluntary Turnover, which declined from 32.9% in FY25 to 19.2% in FY26, 
reflecting the positive impact of targeted interventions and greater workplace flexibility. In response to the FY25 turnover 
rate, we strengthened our employee support framework through greater workplace flexibility for employees facing medical, 
maternity, and personal challenges, and supported through work-from-home arrangements during the year.
Workforce Stability and Engagement
Early-career professionals under 30 record the highest voluntary turnover rate at 23.9% based on the Aon Annual Survey 2025, 
a pattern consistent across the Indian technology sector that reflects the natural exploration of options that characterises 
the early stages of a career rather than dissatisfaction with Tanla specifically. The significant improvement from FY25’s peak 
of 34.3% confirms that structured onboarding, visible career pathways, and early HRBP engagement are having measurable 
effect on a cohort that is inherently more mobile. The 30-to-50 aged cohort, which represents the core execution engine 
of the organisation, recorded its best voluntary retention in three years at a 13.9% rate, and when these experienced 
professionals choose to stay, their institutional knowledge compounds, the quality of the platforms they support improves, 
and the competitive advantage that retained capability represents deepens year by year

Employee Absenteeism
Tanla’s absenteeism rate, measured on a Loss of Pay basis, has remained well below the IT sector average of 1 to 2 percent 
across all three reported years. In FY26, Tanla adopted the LOP-only methodology aligned with S&P Global CSA criterion 3.5.3 
for the first time; prior year figures have been restated on the same basis to enable comparability, though direct year-on-year 
trend conclusions should be read with this methodology transition in mind.
On this basis, the FY26 rate of 0.44% compares with 0.52% in FY25 and 0.51% in FY24. What the three-year picture confirms 
is consistency of performance well below sector norms, with FY26 representing the lowest recorded rate across the period. 
Whether this reflects the cumulative effect of wellbeing investment, workplace flexibility, and proactive health monitoring, 
including tailored pregnancy accommodations and flexible return-to-work arrangements or the impact of the methodology 
refinement itself, cannot be disaggregated from available data alone.

Gender Pay Equity
Tanla’s compensation decisions are based on role complexity, performance, experience, and market benchmarking, 
applied consistently and without regard to gender. Guided by an NRC-approved Total Rewards philosophy and structured 
compensation framework, regular reviews are conducted to identify and address pay gaps as they emerge. The commitment 
to gender pay equity is not a policy statement but a practice embedded in every compensation cycle, with results disclosed 
transparently and interpreted honestly rather than presented selectively.

Methodology Note: Pay parity has been assessed using median compensation data for employee cohorts where the representation of 
both men and women is evaluated to enable a meaningful comparison. Employees have been grouped by function and band to ensure 
comparability of role complexity, responsibilities, and organisational level. Median compensation has been used as the primary measure as 
it reduces the influence of outliers and provides a more representative view of remuneration outcomes within a cohort. Differences observed 
may reflect variations in tenure, experience, specialised skills, leadership responsibilities, and workforce composition within individual 
employee groups.
Tanla’s FY26 pay parity assessment demonstrates strong compensation equity across several comparable employee cohorts. 
Perfect or positive parity was achieved across GTM Bands 3 and 4, Customer Success Band 3, and Corporate Band 2, where 
women-to-men median pay ratios ranged from 100% to 115%. Customer Success Band 2 also recorded a ratio of 92%, indicating 
moderate parity.
Overall, five of the seven comparable cohorts assessed recorded women-to-men pay ratios of 92% or higher, reflecting 
broadly equitable compensation outcomes across customer-facing and corporate functions. In certain cohorts, median 
compensation for women exceeded that of men, demonstrating that remuneration outcomes are driven by role, capability, 
experience, and performance rather than gender.
Variations observed within specific cohorts, particularly in Innovation Band 3 and Corporate Band 4, reflect differences in 
tenure, experience mix, role specialisation, and workforce composition within those employee groups. These cohorts remain 
areas of continued monitoring as part of the organisation’s commitment to equitable compensation practices.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Employee Grievances and POSH
The effectiveness of a grievance mechanism is reflected not only in employees’ willingness to raise concerns, but also in the 
organization’s ability to resolve them. In FY26, 2 employee support and grievance cases were raised across the Tanla Group, 
and both were resolved withing the reporting period, resulting in a 100% resolution rate and no pending cases at year end. 
Figure 4.3: Employee Grievances in FY26
Tanla maintains active Internal Complaints Committees (ICCs) across all office locations, constituted in accordance with the 
Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (prevent, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, with each committee including 
an external member. All ICC members received specialized training during FY26 covering the legal framework, procedural 
responsibilities, and empathetic complaint handling each including an external member. During FY26, one POSH complaint 
was reported and resolved, with no cases pending at year end. 
POSH awareness training continued to be an important component of employee engagement and workplace culture. During 
FY26, 542 men and 202 women participated in POSH training (66.3% and 89.3% of respective workforces).

The assessment expanded its scope to include enhanced risk identification for all permanent and contractual employees.

The FY26 HRDD survey demonstrated strong employee confidence across core human rights and workplace practices. Nearly 
all respondents confirmed unrestricted access to workplace facilities (93.1%) and safe working conditions, including for women 
(96.7%). Awareness of equal opportunity practices remained high, with 90.1% of employees confirming equal opportunities 
regardless of gender and 92.1% regardless of nationality or ethnicity.

from 81.0% in FY25 to 86.5% in FY26, while awareness of compensation terms improved from 87.0% to 89.4%. Awareness of 
non-discrimination policies increased significantly from 73.0% to 86.1%, reflecting the impact of targeted communication and 
awareness initiatives undertaken during the year.
Building on FY25 findings, the organisation strengthened onboarding programmes, employee communications, HR Open 
House sessions, manager engagement, and SPEAKUP awareness initiatives to improve understanding of employee rights, 
performance management processes, and grievance redressal mechanisms.
The survey also highlighted areas requiring continued focus. Awareness of accessibility provisions and support for differently 
abled employees remains limited, with 46.9% of respondents indicating they were unsure whether such measures existed. 
Similarly, uncertainty regarding overtime eligibility and compensatory-off provisions continues to persist. These findings will 
guide FY27 actions, with a focus on strengthening awareness of accessibility initiatives, improving policy communication, and 
enhancing transparency around performance management and employee support mechanisms.

across workplace safety, employment practices, equal opportunity, and employee rights. The findings indicate strong 
confidence in several foundational areas, with 95.8% of respondents confirming safe working conditions and unrestricted 
access to workplace facilities. Awareness of fair treatment and inclusion also remained high, with 91.7% confirming that 
employees are treated fairly without discrimination and 95.8% affirming equal opportunities regardless of nationality or 
ethnicity.
Awareness of key employment practices remained strong, with 87.5% of respondents confirming an understanding of their pay 
and compensation terms, 79.2% acknowledging receipt and understanding of employment contracts, and 87.5% indicating 
awareness of the organisation’s human rights commitments. Confidence in personal data protection practices was also high 
at 91.7%. Building on commitments made in FY25, the organisation continued to expand human rights awareness through 
onboarding programmes, employee communications, and workplace engagement initiatives. These findings will inform FY27 
actions focused on strengthening contractual employee awareness of workplace rights, reporting channels, accessibility 
provisions, and human rights safeguards to ensure that all contractual employees remain informed, protected, and empowered 
within the workplace.
Occupational Health and Safety
Providing a safe, healthy, and supportive workplace is a fundamental responsibility and an important aspect of how we care 
for our people. Our Employee Health and Safety (EHS) Policy guides occupational health and safety practices across all office 
locations and applies to employees, contractors, customers, and visitors. The policy is aligned with applicable regulatory 
requirements and industry best practices and is overseen by senior leadership.
EHS: https:/ /tanlanewwebsite.blob.core.windows.net/assets/files/policy_on_employee_health_and_safety.pdf
Our approach focuses on proactively identifying and managing workplace risks through 
regular inspections, safety audits, and risk assessments. Potential hazards are evaluated 
using structured risk assessment methodologies, with corrective and preventive actions 
implemented wherever required. Safety performance is reviewed periodically to ensure 
that controls remain effective and responsive to changing workplace needs.
Emergency preparedness continued to be a key focus area during FY26. Fire drills 
were conducted across office locations to strengthen emergency response readiness, 
while CPR awareness sessions were delivered to employees to build basic life-saving 
capabilities. Security personnel also underwent periodic training covering workplace 
safety protocols, emergency response procedures, and employee engagement 
practices.
Employees are encouraged to report unsafe conditions, near-miss incidents, and workplace concerns through established 
reporting channels, including the SpeakUp platform. Reported incidents are reviewed and investigated, with corrective 
actions tracked to closure. Quarterly cross-functional safety reviews provide additional oversight and support continuous 
improvement in workplace safety practices.
Our commitment to health and safety extends beyond our workforce to contractors, suppliers, and business partners. Safety 
expectations are incorporated into vendor engagement and procurement processes, reinforcing a shared commitment to 
maintaining safe and responsible workplaces across our value chain.
The effectiveness of this approach is reflected in our performance. During FY26, no workplace injuries, work-related illnesses, 
fatalities, or health and safety complaints were recorded. This extends our record of zero health and safety incidents and zero 
complaints relating to workplace conditions across the last three reporting years.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Labour Practices
Fair, transparent, and responsible labour practices are fundamental to creating a workplace where people can perform, 
grow, and contribute with confidence. Our approach is guided by applicable labour laws, human rights principles, and 
internal policies designed to ensure equitable treatment, safe working conditions, and respect for employee rights across 
both permanent and contractual workforces.
All employees (permanent and contractual) receive remuneration above the statutory minimum wage, and compensation 
practices are periodically reviewed against market benchmarks to support competitiveness and fairness. Employment terms, 
including compensation, benefits, working hours, and leave entitlements, are communicated through formal employment 
contracts and supporting policy frameworks. Employees are also provided access to grievance redressal mechanisms and 
reporting channels that enable concerns to be raised and addressed transparently.
As the organisation continues to evolve in an increasingly AI-enabled environment, we remain committed to supporting 
employees through changing skill requirements. Learning and development initiatives, technical enablement programmes, 
and AI-focused capability-building efforts help employees adapt to emerging technologies and prepare for the future of 
work.
The effectiveness of these practices is reflected in the findings of our Human Rights Due Diligence assessments. In FY26, 
employees reported strong awareness of compensation terms, employment contracts, workplace benefits, and equal 
opportunity practices, reinforcing the organisation’s commitment to responsible employment and workforce wellbeing.
Whistleblower Policy and SPEAKUP Mechanism
A culture of ownership and accountability depends on employees feeling confident that concerns can be raised safely, 
confidentially, and without fear of retaliation. To support this, Tanla maintains its SPEAKUP mechanism, which enables 
employees, contractors, and other stakeholders to report concerns relating to unethical conduct, policy violations, 
discrimination, harassment, or other workplace issues. Reports may be submitted confidentially or anonymously, and all 
concerns are handled in accordance with established governance processes. The organisation maintains a zero-tolerance 
approach to retaliation against any individual who raises a concern in good faith, with protections embedded within both the 
Whistleblower Policy and broader employee governance framework.
Awareness of the SPEAKUP mechanism is reinforced through employee communications, onboarding programmes, and 
periodic sensitisation initiatives, helping ensure that employees understand both how to raise concerns and the protections 
available to them. All concerns reported through the mechanism are reviewed and investigated, with corrective actions 
implemented where required. During FY26, zero pending incidents of harassment, discriminatory conduct, or whistleblower 
retaliation were reported.
05 | Speed
Speed is enabled by a bias for action and a willingness to move forward with confidence. In a technology industry defined by 
constant change, the ability to anticipate market needs, innovate ahead of demand, and execute at pace is a critical source 
of competitive advantage. Whether it is building new capabilities, attracting specialised talent, accelerating career growth, 
or responding to employee feedback, speed is reflected in how quickly ideas become action and action creates impact.
This culture of action extends beyond products and platforms to people practices. By investing in high-quality talent, 
creating opportunities for growth through promotions and internal mobility, and acting swiftly on employee feedback and 
organisational insights, we enable individuals and teams to perform at their highest potential. Speed, therefore is about 
recognising opportunities early and responding decisively while maintaining the quality, trust, and accountability that 
underpin long-term success.
Hiring for the Future: Strengthening Capability at Speed
In a technology industry where customer needs, markets, and technologies evolve rapidly, speed depends on organisational 
readiness. The ability to act decisively is shaped by the strength of the workforce, the depth of capability available across 
critical functions, and the organisation’s ability to build talent ahead of demand. During FY26, Tanla added 324 new employees 
across key business functions, strengthening technical expertise, customer-facing capabilities, and organisational support 
functions to sustain growth and scale.
Hiring continued to be concentrated in Innovation, Improvement, Customer Success, and Go-to-Market functions. Investments 
in Innovation and Improvement teams were made to support the growing demand for next-generation platforms, AI-driven 
solutions, and product enhancements while ensuring that technology infrastructure scaled in line with business requirements. 
Customer Success teams were expanded to support a growing customer base and maintain high standards of service delivery 
and engagement.
GTM hiring focused on accelerating commercialisation of new products and strengthening market presence across strategic 
geographies, including APAC, Southeast Asia, and EMEA. Corporate and Marketing functions were also strengthened to 
support organisational growth, employer branding, governance, and the increasing demands of a global business.

Internal Mobility: Accelerating Growth from Within
Speed is reflected in how quickly organisations innovate, but also in how quickly opportunities reach the people best equipped 
to seize them. Internal mobility enables employees to expand their careers, develop new capabilities, and contribute in 
different ways without having to leave the organisation.
During FY26, 24 employees advanced through internal career mobility mechanisms, including 3 cross-functional transfers and 
21 transitions from contractual to permanent employment. Contractual hiring plays an important role in enabling workforce 
agility, allowing the organisation to access specialised skills quickly and respond to emerging business requirements. As

the success of this model, enabling the organisation to accelerate hiring while retaining talent that has already proven its 
capability and fit within the business. This approach reduces time-to-productivity, strengthens workforce continuity, and 
ensures that opportunities are awarded on demonstrated contribution and potential.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26110Action to Feedback:: The Speed of Improvement
Speed is about how quickly our employee feedback is translated into action. Employee Engagement Surveys (EES) and 
Human Rights Due Diligence (HRDD) assessments provide structured mechanisms for understanding employee experiences, 
identifying areas for improvement, and prioritising actions that strengthen organisational effectiveness.
The FY25 HRDD assessment identified opportunities to improve awareness of non-discrimination policies, employee rights, 
performance management processes, and employee support mechanisms. During FY26, targeted interventions including 
enhanced onboarding, manager engagement, HR Open House sessions, policy communications, and SpeakUp awareness 
initiatives were implemented. These actions contributed to measurable improvements across several indicators, including 
awareness of employment contracts (81.0% to 86.5%), compensation terms (87.0% to 89.4%), non-discrimination policies (73.0% 
to 86.1%), and transparent appraisal processes (57.0% to 65.3%).
Similarly, employee engagement insights led to initiatives such as HR Open Houses, HRBP Connect programmes, Brew 
and Bond sessions, employee wellbeing interventions, leadership engagement forums continue to shape organisational 
priorities and employee experience initiatives. While FY25 recorded an overall engagement score of 73.2%, the FY26 Qualtrics 
assessment adopted a more detailed, multi-dimensional approach to better understand employee experiences across areas 
such as organisational alignment, culture, leadership effectiveness, rewards, and workplace processes. 
The strongest result was Organisation Vision and Goals at 84.8%, exceeding the Qualtrics technology sector benchmark of 
82.6% and demonstrating strong employee alignment with Tanla’s strategic direction. Culture scored 81.8%, marginally below 
the technology sector benchmark of 83.0%, reflecting a year of embedding the organisation’s five operating values into daily 
practice. Process and Tools emerged as the clearest opportunity area at 77.2%, compared to the technology sector benchmark 
of 85.0%, highlighting opportunities to simplify workflows, enhance employee experience, and improve operational efficiency. 
These findings continue to inform FY27 priorities, ensuring that employee feedback is translated into targeted actions that 
strengthen engagement, productivity, and organisational effectiveness.
These findings demonstrate a commitment to acting. By converting employee feedback into targeted interventions and 
measurable improvement plans, the organisation continues to strengthen a culture where insights lead to action and action 
leads to progress.
Across talent acquisition, career growth, internal mobility, and employee engagement, the common thread is responsiveness. 
By anticipating capability needs, creating opportunities for advancement, and acting on employee insights, Tanla is building 
an organisation that can adapt quickly without compromising quality, trust, or accountability. This ability to learn, respond, 
and execute at pace strengthens both employee experience and organisational performance, ensuring that speed remains 
a defining characteristic of how we create value.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Conclusion
The Tanla Human Capital is the engine that powers every product we build, every customer we serve, and every opportunity 
we pursue.
FY26 marks an important milestone in the evolution of our people philosophy. The foundations established through the 3Cs 
Framework and strengthened through GROW have matured into the Tanla Foundry’s five core values, Innovation, Impact, 
Excellence, Ownership, and Speed. These values are no longer principles that guide behaviour; they are increasingly visible in 
the outcomes the organisation delivers.
• Innovation is reflected in a workforce where nearly 80% of employees operate in STEM roles and where AI is becoming 
embedded into the way work gets done. 
• Impact is evident in the talent, expertise, and customer-centric capabilities that enable us to serve enterprises, regulators, 
telcos, and millions of end users at scale.
• Excellence is reinforced through continuous learning, strong internal leadership pipelines, and a performance culture that 
rewards contribution and growth.
• Ownership is demonstrated through high levels of employee trust, internal mobility, career progression, and long-term 
commitment to the organisation. 
• Speed is visible in our ability to build capabilities ahead of demand, deploy talent where it is needed most, and convert 
feedback into action with urgency and intent.
The true measure of a high-performance culture is what it consistently delivers. A highly skilled workforce. Record-low 
voluntary turnover.. Strong leadership continuity. Expanding diversity. Sustained investment in learning. Safe and inclusive 
workplaces. These outcomes are not independent achievements. Together, they are evidence of a people system designed 
to compound capability, strengthen resilience, and create enduring competitive advantage.
As technology, AI, and customer expectations continue to reshape our industry, our greatest differentiator will not be just the 
platforms we build, but the people who build them. By continuing to invest in talent, leadership, and culture, Tanla is building 
a future-ready organisation equipped to define it.
High performance is the outcome of exceptional people united by a shared purpose, empowered by shared values, 
and committed to creating extraordinary impact.

Innovation has always been intentional and purpose-led at Tanla. 
We build where the problem is hardest, stakes are highest, and 
gap between what exists and what is needed is widest. Over three 
decades, that conviction has shaped every platform we have built, 
patent we filed, and market we entered.
The world went digital faster than anyone anticipated. A billion 
Indians came online. Enterprises moved their most critical customer 
interactions to digital channels. Financial transactions, identity 
verification, healthcare access, and daily commerce all migrated 
to the connected world, bringing with them unprecedented 
convenience and risk. Every new digital touchpoint created a new 
surface for fraud. Every channel that enterprises adopted to reach 
their customers became a channel that bad actors sought to exploit. 
The digital citizen, connected but not always protected, became the 
target. Tanla exists to change that. We do not treat digital safety as 
a feature or a compliance requirement. It is a foundational design 
principle embedded into every platform we build, every deployment 
we scale, and every problem we choose to solve.
In FY26, that purpose found its fullest expression yet. We took trusted 
communications global, extended our compliance infrastructure 
into voice, deepened our enterprise engagement platforms, and 
accelerated the pace of our patent activity to its highest level in our

a communications platform business into an AI-native enterprise

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY261)Wisely.ai Taking Trusted Communications 
Global 
Digital fraud has become one of the most pervasive 
threats to consumer trust in the connected world. Global 
cybercrime costs reached USD 10.5 trillion annually in 2025 
(Cybersecurity Ventures). A significant share of this threat is 
delivered through trusted channels such as SMS, voice, and 
OTT, where billions of malicious communications exploit the 
confidence users place in the networks they rely on every 
day. Across Southeast Asia and beyond, billions of malicious 
communications are delivered each year via SMS, voice, 
and OTT channels, exploiting the trust that users place 
in the networks they rely on daily. Wisely.ai was purpose-
built to address this challenge. It operates at the network 
layer, assessing and acting on every communication before 
it reaches the user, at national scale, in real time. Cloud-
agnostic and deployable via API into existing infrastructure, 
Wisely.ai requires no proprietary hardware and no disruption 
to legacy systems, making it available to any telco, in any 
geography, from day one.
Wisely.ai operates across three tightly integrated layers. 
1. The Data Layer provides the foundation: ISO certified, 
GDPR compliant, and built on secured AI infrastructure 
that processes real-time traffic with full adherence to 
local data sovereignty requirements. 
2. The AI Layer runs four capabilities in parallel: agentic 
decision-making, validation, self-learning, and 
autonomous operation. Together, they deliver a precise 
verdict on every communication event in under 10 
milliseconds, without human intervention. 
3. The Product Layer turns intelligence into action. A 
single API spans network protection, mobile app and 
SDK integration, user identity, and a unified experience 
panel, making deployment seamless across any telco 
environment. Underpinning it all is Wise Albert, our 
generative AI engine, which makes the platform more 
precise with every communication it analyses.
4. This year, we deployed Wisely.ai with Indosat Ooredoo 
Hutchison, Indonesia’s leading telecom operator, and 
brought real-time spam and scam protection to nearly 
100 million subscribers. It is a landmark moment for 
Tanla, and a powerful demonstration that the trust 
infrastructure we have built in India is ready for the 
world, structured as SaaS engagement with measurable 
outcomes at its core.
The platform delivers protection through five purpose-built 
solutions:
• Anti-Spam  solves the noise problem at its root. We 
deploy sender reputation scoring, traffic profiling, and 
behavioural pattern detection to identify and neutralise 
unsolicited bulk communications across SMS, VoLTE, and 
VoIP before they reach the subscriber. Operating at both 
the network and application layer across Android and 
iOS, the solution requires no action from the user and no 
change to existing infrastructure, filtering at scale while 
ensuring every legitimate communication gets through.
• Anti-Scam  goes further, understanding the intent 
behind every communication rather than matching it 
against known patterns. Built on our patented Wisely ATP 
heritage, it applies NLP and semantic analysis to detect 
urgency cues, misdirection tactics, and fraudulent calls-
to-action. Every embedded URL is inspected through 
AI-driven sandboxing, and computer vision scans 
image-based messages for visual brand impersonation, 
catching attacks that text-only filters are simply not 
built to see. When a threat is confirmed, the response is 
immediate: calls are flagged with red-coded alerts and malicious URLs are redirected to safe landing pages 
before the subscriber can interact with them. Across 
more than 500 billion messages scanned annually, Anti-
Scam operates with efficacy exceeding 99% and false 
positive rates held below 0.5%.
• Identity+ i.e., Verified Business , addresses a different 
but equally consequential problem: the trust deficit 
that causes legitimate enterprise communications 
to go unanswered. When a verified business calls, the 
subscriber sees the authenticated brand name, logo, 
verified badge, and purpose of the call before deciding 
whether to pick up. No app download required. No 
ambiguity about who is calling or why. For enterprises, 
this means higher answer rates, reduced outbound 
waste, and protection from impersonation. For operators, 
it converts voice from a commodity channel into an 
identity-enabled service with measurable commercial 
value.
• Threat Intelligence  operates as a two-way federated 
exchange, connecting telcos, banks, regulators, and 
enterprises into a single, continuously enriched defence 
network. Through secure APIs, every participant can 
query confirmed fraud intelligence, verify numbers 
against a live repository of over 1.2 million identified 
threats, and contribute signals back into the ecosystem 
in real time. A bank flagging a suspicious transaction can 
instantly validate the originating number against known 
fraud history. A telco detecting a new scam sender 
pushes that signature to every connected participant 
within minutes. No single organisation sees the full picture 
alone. Together, they do.
Wise Albert is the analytics and insight engine that sits 
across the entire platform, cutting through every layer and 
every solution. Designed specifically for CXO-level decision-
making, it surfaces the intelligence that senior leaders need 
to act on, converting complex, high-volume operational 
data into clear strategic insight without requiring technical 
interpretation. It analyses patterns at scale, surfaces 
emerging risks before they materialise, identifies gaps in 
coverage, and translates the full breadth of platform activity 
into a coherent view of the threat landscape, ensuring 
that the decisions made at the top of an organisation are 
grounded in the most precise understanding of what is 
happening across their networks at any given moment. 
Where the other four solutions intercept and block, Wise 
Albert interprets and anticipates.
In FY26, our engineering and data strategy centered on 
unlocking the power of AI-driven analytics to manage 
high-throughput telecom traffic at an unprecedented 
scale. By integrating advanced analytics within the 
Wisely.ai platform, we have optimized our architecture 
to process immense volumes of signaling data 
with unparalleled speed and precision. Even as we 
aggressively scale these high-throughput capabilities, 
our foundational commitment to data-blind, zero-
trust infrastructure ensures that subscriber privacy 
remains absolute. This synergy of high-performance 
processing and secure AI represents the cornerstone 
of our intellectual capital, delivering verifiable trust and 
operational excellence across the ecosystem.KVP Reddy
SVP, Engineering

4) Trubloq
Trubloq, our blockchain-based DLT platform and the world’s 
largest of its kind, continued to advance in FY26 with a defining 
focus on the Telecom Commercial Communications Customer 
Preference Regulations (TCCCPR), the regulatory framework 
governing enterprise-to-consumer voice communication in 
India. As TRAI intensified its mandate to eliminate fraud and 
restore consumer trust, Trubloq emerged as the platform 
of choice for enabling compliant, verified, and traceable 
communication at scale.
The most significant development this year was the launch of 
the dedicated 1600 number series for service and transactional 
communication in the financial sector, deployed via Trubloq. 
The 1600 series assigns verified, exclusive number ranges 
to regulated financial institutions including banks, NBFCs, insurance companies, mutual fund houses, stock brokers, 
payment aggregators, and RBI-regulated entities, giving 
consumers a recognisable, trusted voice channel they can 
answer with confidence. By restricting access to authorised 
entities only, the series directly addresses identity theft, 
phishing, KYC fraud, and loan scams, while enabling authentic 
OTP delivery and eliminating fake bank and insurance calls. 
Every call is tracked and verified through Trubloq’s DLT 
infrastructure, with blockchain-based immutable records 
delivering end-to-end traceability, real-time fraud detection, 
and consumer grievance redressal, backed by non-compliance 
penalties that ensure accountability across the ecosystem.
The impact is tangible across every stakeholder. Financial 
institutions have seen higher call pickup rates, reduced fraud 
liability, stronger brand trust, and fewer customer complaints. 
Consumers engage with greater confidence, knowing a 1600 
series call is legitimate, verified, and safe. Regulators gain 
the oversight, fraud monitoring, and compliance tracking 
that a maturing digital economy demands. Trubloq is not just 
enabling the 1600 series, it is laying the foundation for a new 
era of verified voice communication in India, with the framework 
built to scale across all business sectors as adoption deepens.
As TCCCPR continues to evolve, Trubloq remains the critical 
infrastructure layer that enterprises, telcos, and regulators 
depend on, combining blockchain-grade auditability, 
AI-powered intelligence, and regulatory depth to keep pace 
with every new mandate.
Compliance and traceability create the conditions for trust. 
What enterprises choose to do within those conditions, how 
they engage, convert, and retain customers, is where our 
enterprise engagement platforms come in.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Conclusion: Building the Infrastructure for 
What Comes Next
The platforms described in this chapter share a common 
ambition: to make digital communication safer, smarter, and 
more valuable for every participant in the ecosystem. In FY26, 
we made significant progress towards that ambition, and in 
doing so, took a defining step in our evolution as a company. 
Our CPaaS business continues to scale through Karix and 
ValueFirst, serving over 2,500 enterprises across messaging, 
voice, and conversational AI. In parallel, Tanla is pivoting 
decisively towards becoming an AI-native platform company, 
one where intelligence is not a feature layered onto existing 
products but the core of how every platform we build operates, 
decides, and improves. The frontier continues to move, and we 
are moving with it.
Silent authentication represents one of the most significant 
near-term opportunities in trusted communications. By 
verifying a user’s identity seamlessly in the background, using 
network-level signals rather than OTPs or passwords, silent 
authentication eliminates friction at the moment of highest 
drop-off, without compromising security. As enterprises seek 
to reduce abandonment in onboarding and transaction flows, 
and as regulators push for stronger identity assurance, this 
capability positions us at the intersection of user experience 
and trust infrastructure.
The broader network API ecosystem represents a longer-term 
ambition, one that is reshaping how the intelligence of the 
telecom layer is made available to enterprises and developers 
in standardised, programmable ways. Our deep integration 
with operator infrastructure, built over nearly three decades, 
positions us to be a natural bridge between the network layer 
and the enterprise, translating raw network intelligence into 
actionable, consent-driven communication capabilities.
The thread that connects silent authentication, network APIs, 
and every platform described in this chapter is the same thread 
that has guided our innovation from the beginning: the belief 
that the most important problems in digital communication 
are problems of trust, and that solving them at scale, with 
precision and purpose, is a responsibility we have chosen to 
take seriously.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Infrastructure Modernisation, Green Data 
Centres and E-Waste Management 
As the scale and complexity of our services grow, so do the 
requirements on our infrastructure. To keep pace with customer 
needs and evolving digital requirements, We have modernised 
our systems to increase efficiency, sustainability and better 
prepare for disruption. This year we have consolidated 
infrastructure, upgraded servers, adopted green data 
centre practices, and also created a structured approach to 
responsible disposal of hardware that neared the end of life, 
thereby delivering measurable outcomes across cost, energy 
and environmental performance.
Server Upgrades and Data Centre 
Consolidation 
In FY26, Tanla initiated the consolidation of its data centre 
infrastructure into a single-floor architecture across key 
facilities, significantly reducing logistical complexity 
and improving interconnectivity between systems. This 
consolidation is ongoing and continues to inform infrastructure 
planning.
Beyond the direct energy and cost savings, consolidation 
delivered a meaningful indirect benefit: a significant reduction 
in the need for physical intervention by infrastructure and 
operations teams. Fewer racks and a simplified single-floor 
layout mean fewer routine inspection visits, reduced on-site 
troubleshooting requirements, and lower dependency on 
manual checks to verify rack health, cabling integrity and 
cooling status. Where engineers previously needed to be 
physically present to diagnose or resolve issues, automation 
and remote monitoring now handle the majority of these tasks. 
This has freed infrastructure staff to redirect their time toward 
higher-value engineering, platform reliability and proactive 
capacity planning work. If tracked, the reduction in the number 
of scheduled and unscheduled site visits would represent a 
quantifiable productivity gain, we will look to report this metric 
in future disclosures. 
90% of legacy physical servers have now migrated to 
virtualised environments. This has reduced physical hardware 
dependency by approximately 25% and significantly lowered 
power and cooling requirements across our offices. Chassis-
based infrastructure using integrated power and cooling 
modules has been deployed, enabling capacity growth without 
proportional increases in energy consumption. Internal LAN 
infrastructure was also upgraded to 10G networking across 
major platforms, resulting in improved system responsiveness 
and throughput for digital services. Virtualisation has also 
contributed to the same indirect productivity benefit, with 
fewer physical servers to maintain, the volume of hands-on 
intervention required from the infrastructure team has declined, 
allowing engineers to operate at greater leverage and focus 
on work that directly advances platform performance and 
customer outcomes. 
The organisation transitioned from rated power billing to 
metered, actual power consumption billing, ensuring charges 
reflect real-time utilisation rather than theoretical peak 
capacity. This shift to consumption-based metering has 
improved visibility into workload-level energy usage, enabled 
more accurate infrastructure cost attribution, and supported 
ongoing optimisation of power allocation across environments. 
The transition resulted in monthly savings of approximately 
12–15% on power costs. Bandwidth rightsizing initiatives further 
reduced blocking of excess capacity, delivering additional 
annual savings of approximately 8% on connectivity costs.Green Data Centres 
Our network infrastructure is deployed in green data centres 
that leverage renewable energy sources and energy-
efficient technologies. Our data centre strategy is guided by 
a commitment to reducing power usage effectiveness (PUE) 
and minimising cooling load through intelligent infrastructure 
design. The migration from physical to virtualised environments 
has been central to achieving these end goals, by consolidating 
workloads onto fewer, higher-utilisation servers, we have 
materially reduced the energy footprint associated with 
operating our platforms at scale. 
Chassis-based integrated power and cooling modules reduce 
redundant energy consumption compared to discrete server 
deployments. Continuous audits of our data centre footprint 
ensure that capacity provisioning remains aligned with actual 
demand, avoiding excess-provisioning and associated energy 
wastage. These practices reflect our commitment to operating 
infrastructure that is not only performant but environmentally 
responsible. 
Responsible E-Waste Disposal 
As legacy hardware has retired through our virtualisation 
programme, we ensure that decommissioned equipment is 
disposed of responsibly. All e-waste is channelled through 
certified recycling partners in compliance with the E-Waste 
(Management) Rules, 2022, and extended producer 
responsibility (EPR) obligations. Form 6 manifests are obtained 
for every disposal, maintaining a complete and auditable 
chain of custody from asset retirement through to certified 
recycling. 
This year we completed a consolidated group-wide e-waste 
disposal cycle — the planned cycle flagged in the FY25 BRSR 
disclosure, covering accumulated hardware across group 
entities. A total of 12,970 KG (12.97 MT) of e-waste was disposed 
through an MPCB-licensed recycler. 
Tanla’s infrastructure modernization journey is focused 
on building a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable 
on-premises technology foundation. Through container 
orchestration, automated workload scheduling, 
and infrastructure optimization technologies, we 
are improving resource utilization while reducing 
dependency on excess hardware capacity.
This modernization is helping us lower energy 
consumption, reduce data centre space requirements, 
and minimize the carbon footprint of our operations. 
It reflects our commitment to operational excellence, 
resilience, and long-term environmental responsibility.”Pradeep Siwach
Associate Director, IT & Security

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Process Technology Enhancements 
We invest in technology infrastructure upgrades on an 
ongoing basis, with a focus on operational efficiency. 
Containerisation through Kubernetes and cloud-native 
platforms has improved resource utilisation. Infrastructure is 
predominantly on-premises, with selective hybrid connectivity

Custom-built dashboards provide real-time monitoring of 
key performance indicators, allowing teams to identify and

Quality Management System 
Tanla implements a comprehensive Quality Management 
System (QMS) designed to drive consistency and customer 
satisfaction across all business functions and software 
development processes. The framework is aligned with 
ISO 9001:2015 and CMMi Level 3 principles, ensuring that 
practices are standardised, outcomes are measurable, and 
improvements are continuous rather than reactive. The QMS 
connects teams, workflows and technology into a single 
delivery model, built to meet global standards and keep pace 
with evolving customer needs. 
Information Security Management System 
We maintain a comprehensive Information Security 
Management System (ISMS) to protect the confidentiality, 
integrity and availability of data across our platforms. The 
ISMS is aligned with ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and the 
Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), with security 
integrated into every layer from product design to operations. 
The system is built around risk-based controls, proactive 
threat detection, and a security-aware culture across the 
organisation. The outcome is secure, reliable service delivery 
to customers at scale.
Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) 
Tanla maintains a centralised GRC framework to monitor 
and manage regulatory, contractual and internal security 
requirements. The framework adheres to The framework 
adheres to ISO 27001, ISO 20000, ISO 31000, SOC 2 Type 2, GDPR 
and the DPDPA. Risk assessments cover both IT infrastructure 
and business operations. Controls are implemented and 
monitored through the ISMS, supported by internal audits and 
external assessments. The Risk Management Committee inter 
alia, provides senior-level oversight of information security 
issues.  
Key components of the GRC framework include: 
• Enterprise Risk Register and Treatment Plan:  All identified 
risks are tracked in a centralised register, with mitigation 
plans aligned to business priorities. Governance is 
structured across four roles: the ISMS Forum provides 
oversight, the ISMS Officer handles policy and monitoring, 
Department Heads execute, and the ISMS Auditor drives 
continuous improvement. 
• Security Policies and Procedures:  Documented policies and 
standard operating procedures establish the foundation 
for operational security and regulatory compliance. The 
ISMS Forum and Department Heads are jointly responsible 
for consistent implementation. 
• Regular Compliance Audits:  Internal and external audits 
assess adherence to organisational policies and regulatory 
requirements. Where gaps are identified, action plans are 
developed by the ISMS Auditor and tracked by the ISMS 
Forum. • Data Protection Officer (DPO) Oversight: The DPO ensures 
organisation-wide compliance with data protection 
regulations including GDPR and DPDPA. This includes 
implementing privacy-by-design principles, conducting 
impact assessments and managing data subject rights.
Identity and Access Management (IAM) 
We maintain strict control over access to our systems and 
applications through a comprehensive IAM framework. This 
includes identity federation, role-based access controls 
(RBAC) and multi-factor authentication (MFA). Privileged 
accounts are managed through a centralised Privileged 
Access Management (PAM) solution. During FY26, IAM was 
further strengthened through Microsoft Single Sign-On (SSO) 
via Azure Active Directory, centralised identity management 
across approximately all corporate employees, and integration 
with the organisation’s BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) policy to 
extend access controls to employee-owned devices.  
Key elements of the IAM framework are: 
• Least Privilege and Segregation of Duties:  Users are 
granted only the minimum access necessary to perform 
their roles, reducing the risk of unauthorised actions. 
• Just-in-Time Access Control:  Access to critical systems 
is granted only when needed. Temporary access is tightly 
controlled and monitored. 
• User Lifecycle Management:  User accounts are managed 
from creation to deactivation, with access aligned to 
employment status and responsibilities. 
• Periodic Access Reviews:  Access rights are reviewed 
regularly to confirm that permissions remain appropriate 
as roles change. 
Secure Architecture and Network Security 
Tanla’s network and systems are designed around secure 
architecture principles. Network traffic is segregated, 
encrypted and continuously monitored through WAF, BOT 
protection, DDoS mitigation, Next-Generation Firewalls 
(NGFW) and Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems 
(IDS/IPS). During FY26, the internal LAN infrastructure was 
upgraded to 10G networking across major platforms including 
Trubloq 2.0, Voice Agentic, SMSC and MaaP, improving system 
responsiveness and throughput for digital services. 
Key components of our security architecture are: 
• WAF, BOT Protection and DDoS: Web and API resources are 
protected against internet-facing cyber-attacks through 
layered filtering and rate-limiting controls. 
• Network Micro-Segmentation:  Network segments are 
isolated to limit the spread of potential breaches and 
reduce the overall attack surface. 
• Firewall and IPS/IDS Configuration:  Firewalls and intrusion 
prevention systems are configured to detect and block 
malicious activity at the perimeter. 
• API Gateway Security Controls:  Security measures at the 
API gateway protect against threats targeting application 
interfaces.
Data Protection & Encryption 
We implement encryption protocols across data in transit 
and at rest to protect customer trust and meet regulatory 
compliance requirements. All sensitive and personal data is 
managed in accordance with Privacy by Design principles, with 
privacy safeguarded at every stage of data processing.

• TLS 1.2+ for Data in Transit: Secure transport layer protocols 
encrypt data as it moves across networks, protecting it 
from interception.

Threat Detection, SOC & Endpoint Protection 
Our Security Operations Centre (SOC) operates 24/7, using 
an integrated SIEM system and Threat Intelligence platforms

monitoring across user devices, servers and workloads. During

real-time anomaly detection and diagnostics across critical 
infrastructure. 
Key capabilities include: 
• Centralised SOC Operations with Real-Time Alerts:  The

responded to through log correlation and actionable threat

• EDR Deployment Across Critical Assets:  Endpoint 
protection covers all user devices, servers and critical 
infrastructure, with Cortex XDR now deployed as the

• Attack Surface Management and Behavioural Analytics:

with behavioural analytics used to identify anomalous 
patterns. 
• Firmware Management and Security Patching:  Firmware

regularly applied across critical systems including Trubloq, 
Wisely Ai, SMSC, Voice and MaaP, reducing vulnerability 
exposure. 
• Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and Incident Reporting:  
Incidents are analysed in detail, with structured reporting to 
support effective resolution and prevention of recurrence. 
• Cybersecurity Drills and Tabletop Simulations:  Drills 
and simulations are conducted regularly to test incident 
response preparedness. During FY26, a full-scale cyber 
crisis tabletop exercise was conducted with EY. 
Business Continuity Plan & Disaster Recovery 
(BCP/DR) 
Tanla’s Business Continuity Plan (BCP) is designed to maintain 
service delivery during unforeseen events. It applies across all 
employees, subsidiaries, contractors and vendors with access 
to our infrastructure, ensuring a coordinated approach to crisis 
management and recovery. The BCP incorporates information security principles to uphold 
the confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) of information 
assets during disruptions. It is reviewed and updated 
bi-annually, incorporating evolving threat landscapes, 
regulatory changes, and insights from both simulations and 
actual incidents. The CISO of the organization leads oversight 
and compliance enforcement. 
Key components of our BCP are as follows:
• Risk Assessment:  Assessments are conducted regularly 
to identify and evaluate potential risks and vulnerabilities 
across the business. 
• Recovery Strategies:  Scenario-based plans address 
cyber-attacks, technology failures, operational disruptions 
and natural calamities, with defined response procedures 
for each. 
• Resource Allocation:  Critical personnel, technology assets 
and infrastructure resources are provisioned in advance to 
support continuity during a disruption. 
• Testing and Validation:  The BCP is tested every 180 
days through structured simulations, drills and scenario-
based exercises to validate preparedness and response 
effectiveness. 
Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM) 
Tanla’s TPRM framework ensures that all vendors and 
partners, particularly those with access to sensitive data or 
critical operations, meet the company’s security standards. A 
comprehensive onboarding process requires detailed security 
evaluations. These include review of certifications such as 
ISO 27001 and SOC 2, as well as relevant penetration testing 
reports. 
Key components of our TPRM program: 
• Vendor Security Questionnaire:  Prior to onboarding, each 
third party is required to complete a structured security 
assessment covering data protection controls, access 
management practices, incident response capabilities 
and overall compliance posture. This assessment forms 
the baseline against which ongoing vendor risk is tracked 
and reassessed. 
• Contractual Security Clauses:  Legal agreements include 
Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) and Standard 
Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to enforce data privacy and 
protection obligations. 
• Annual Third-Party Reassessment:  Risk evaluations 
are conducted annually to confirm that vendors remain 
compliant with evolving security requirements. 
• Continuous Monitoring of Critical Vendors:  High-risk 
vendors are subject to continuous oversight through 
automated tools and periodic manual reviews conducted  
on quarterly basis to detect and address emerging security 
concerns.

Cyber Crisis Drill Tabletop Exercise 
In FY26, Tanla conducted a cyber crisis simulation moderated 
by a leading Big 4 firm, bringing together 22 senior participants 
across the group — including CXOs, the CTO, Chief AI, Data and 
Analytics Officer, General Counsel, and senior leaders from 
cybersecurity, engineering, IT and finance. 
The scenario simulated a ransomware attack originating 
from a targeted phishing email directed at the HR function. 
The exercise unfolded across four days of simulated time, 
with escalating phases designed to test the organisation’s 
response at each stage. 
Senior leadership participated in structured cyber war 
tabletop exercises designed to test organisational decision-
making, cross-functional coordination and crisis response 
under realistic attack scenarios. Exercises are built around 
multi-phase threat simulations — spanning initial compromise, 
lateral movement, data exposure and regulatory notification 
— reflecting the complexity of real-world incidents that 
organisations of our scale may face. The focus is not on the 
technical mechanics of an attack, but on how leadership 
identifies, escalates, contains and communicates during 
a high-pressure incident. Each exercise concludes with a 
structured debrief, identifying gaps in response protocols 
and informing updates to controls, playbooks and escalation 
frameworks. Key takeaways from the exercise: 
The exercise reinforced that cyber incidents demand cross-
functional coordination, not just an IT response. It also 
identified specific areas for continued focus. Speed of initial 
detection was one. Clarity of internal communication during 
a crisis was another. Readiness for regulatory and media 
engagement was tested and reemphasized on areas that 
requiring ongoing attention. The exercise also underlined the 
importance of repeating such drills regularly as personnel and 
strategies evolve. 
The drill was designed around real-world attack scenarios that 
have affected major global companies. All incidents simulated 
during the exercise were drawn from documented breaches, 
adapted to our operating environment. 
Secure Software Development Lifecycle 
(SSDLC) 
Tanla follows a SSDLC that integrates security at every stage, 
guided by DevSecOps principles. Security is embedded 
into development and operations from the outset, with 
collaboration between teams to maintain continuous 
oversight. 
The lifecycle begins with secure requirements gathering, 
where both functional and security controls are identified to 
meet business and regulatory needs. In the design phase, 
threat modelling is used to identify risks and define mitigation 
strategies. Development follows secure coding standards, with 
peer reviews and static code analysis integrated into each 
release cycle. The CI/CD pipeline incorporates automated 
tools for code review and vulnerability scanning. 
QA emphasises security testing through static and dynamic 
analysis. Pre-production simulates real-world deployment 
scenarios with vulnerability assessments and configuration 
validation. Production environments enforce hardened security 
controls with continuous monitoring and incident response 
readiness. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) restricts access 
to critical systems, and audit trails support traceability and 
compliance across all stages. 
The SSDLC is aligned with ISO 27001 and GDPR, ensuring 
regulatory compliance throughout the development process. 
AI Product Development Lifecycle (AI PDLC) 
Tanla’s SSDLC is further strengthened by an internally defined 
AI PDLC, a structured framework governing how AI is integrated 
from ideation through deployment. Unlike ad hoc AI adoption, 
the AI PDLC codifies where and how AI augments each stage 
of the development process: from requirement refinement and 
architecture reviews, to code generation, test coverage, and 
deployment monitoring. 
Across every stage, AI tooling is not optional — it is embedded 
in daily workflows. Cursor AI, Claude, and GitHub Copilot are 
standard instruments across our engineering and product 
teams. This represents institutional ownership of AI practice, 
not just tool familiarity: a deliberate, governance-led 
approach that ensures AI is used consistently, responsibly, and 
with measurable impact on delivery quality. 
The AI PDLC covers five stages of the development 
process.  
1. Ideation and requirements, where AI assists in refining 
specifications and identifying gaps early.  
=== page 127 ===
#TanlaIntegratedReportFY261262. Architecture review, where AI tooling supports design 
validation and risk assessment.  
3. Code generation, where Cursor AI, Claude, and GitHub 
Copilot accelerate development while enforcing coding 
standards.  
4. Test coverage, where AI-powered tools expand scenario 
coverage and identify edge cases faster than manual 
methods alone. 
5. Deployment monitoring, where AI-assisted observability 
tools enable proactive detection and response. 
The impact is felt most directly by the people doing the work. 
By absorbing repetitive, low-value tasks, the framework frees 
engineers and product teams to focus on higher-order problem 
solving and creative execution. New team members ramp 
faster, experienced engineers operate at greater leverage, 
and the capability floor rises across every team, not just the 
ceiling. 
The AI PDLC also creates a shared language and common 
practice across teams, the hallmark of a high-performance 
culture that scales its best habits, not just its headcount. This 
is not an experiment. It is standard operating practice, making 
our people genuinely AI-native in how they build, not just in 
what they build.

Data Privacy & Data Security 
Safeguarding data privacy and security is central to our 
operations. The organisation aligns with GDPR, DPDPA, and 
LGPD. Products and practices are designed to meet the 
standards required by each framework. A comprehensive 
policy framework, complemented by technical controls, 
protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) of 
customer and stakeholder information. • Policy Framework & Compliance:  Our Data Security & 
Privacy Policy is reviewed and updated regularly. It reflects 
emerging threats and current compliance requirements, 
and provides lifecycle protection for sensitive information. 
• Data Protection & Collection:  Lawful data collection 
practices are enforced, with explicit consent obtained 
where required. Data handling upholds confidentiality and 
limits access based on business need. 
• Privacy Compliance & Data Processing:  Privacy-by-design 
is embedded into operational processes. Strict retention 
and deletion practices are adhered to in accordance with 
the applicable regulations and business requirements. 
• Access Control & Data Storage: Data access is limited to 
authorised personnel through RBAC and the Principle of 
Least Privilege. All archived data is encrypted whether on 
cloud or on premises. 
• Data Encryption & Security:  AES-256 encryption is enforced 
for data at rest. TLS 1.2+ is used for data in transit. These 
practices ensure that communication channels and 
storage platforms meet required cryptographic standards. 
• Data Sharing & Compliance:  Data is anonymized or 
pseudonymized if exported to protect identities. Third 
parties and vendors are contractually required to adhere 
to Tanla’s data privacy and security policies. 
Incident Response Plan (IRP) 
Tanla’s Incident Response Plan provides a structured 
approach to managing cybersecurity incidents. The IRP 
defines procedures across five stages, designed to minimise 
the impact on operations and customer trust. 
• Detection & Identification:  Real-time security monitoring 
and threat intelligence enable rapid identification of 
incidents as they occur. 
• Containment:  Affected systems are isolated immediately 
to prevent escalation and protect unaffected assets. 
• Eradication:  Root causes are analysed and eliminated to 
ensure vulnerabilities are fully addressed and do not recur. 
• Recovery : Affected systems and data are restored 
securely. Normal operations are resumed with integrity and 
availability confirmed before services go live. 
• Post-Incident Review:  Each incident is followed by a 
structured assessment to identify gaps and strengthen 
future preparedness. 
Technology and Security Integration 
Our technology stack is built to make Business Continuity 
Planning (BCP) and Incident Response Planning (IRP) 
operationally effective, with security, recovery and 
observability embedded into the infrastructure itself. 
• Shift-Left Security & Container Security:  Security practices 
are integrated early in the development lifecycle. Tools 
such as Anchore, Trivy and Docker Scout provide real-time 
vulnerability assessment at the container level. 
• Automated Data Backups:  Geographically distributed 
backups are maintained and automated. This method 
ensures data availability and swift recovery during 
disruptions. 
• High-Availability (HA) Queuing:  Reliable queuing 
mechanisms prevent message loss and maintain consistent 
service performance.

Natural capital encompasses the world’s stocks of natural assets 
soil, water, air, and all living organisms that underpin economic 
activity and human well-being. As a software and communications 
platform company, Tanla’s direct resource intensity is lower than 
that of manufacturing or extractive industries. Our obligation to 
manage these resources responsibly, however, is no less significant. 
The functions under natural capital are aligned with the Tanla’s 
objective to reduce ecological footprint, mitigate climate-related 
risks, and advance its transition toward a resource-efficient 
future. Climate action is not a compliance exercise; it is a discipline 
embedded in how our offices are designed, procured, and operated 
each day. 
In FY26, we treated environmental stewardship as a workplace 
standard across our network of seven offices in five Indian cities. 
The year was defined by the transition from intent to operating 
discipline. Footfall-based electricity protocols were implemented, 
replacing default-on operating assumptions. We transitioned to 
an Integrated Facility Management model across both are offices 
in Hyderabad and our office in Mumbai, replacing location-specific 
vendor arrangements with a single partner operating under unified 
standards and accountability. By bringing housekeeping, technical 
maintenance, security, and front-of-house operations under one 
management framework, we established consistent environmental, 
safety, and operational practices across locations. This approach 
has strengthened waste segregation, energy management, water 
conservation, and workplace hygiene standards while improving 
coordination, accountability, and service responsiveness. 
Initiatives that began as pilots in prior years, including occupancy-
calibrated food ordering, restricted printing protocols, and digital 
cafeteria feedback mechanisms, became embedded practices in 
FY26. Through regular employee feedback on food quality, menu Contribution to UN SDGs 
=== page 131 ===
#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26130preferences, and consumption patterns, admin teams make 
more informed planning decisions, improving employee 
satisfaction while minimising excess preparation and food 
waste. This data-driven approach supports both resource 
efficiency and workplace experience objectives. 
Across each of these campuses, the choices we make are 
intentional and cumulative. From the materials we procure 
to the infrastructure we operate, from the water we draw to 
the waste we dispose of, we have consistently chosen the 
more responsible option. That pattern of deliberate choices 
sustained across seven offices over multiple years, is what 
environmental stewardship means for an organisation of our 
kind. 
Scope 1 emissions declined for the second consecutive year, 
falling from 193.94 tCO2e in FY24 to 102.59 tCO2e in FY25 to 
88.43 tCO2e in FY26, driven by the complete elimination 
of diesel generator use at our Hyderabad SEZ campus and 
a systematic fleet renewal programme under which ageing 
vehicles were replaced with newer, fuel-efficient models. 
Scope 2 emissions remained broadly flat at 1,090.75 tCO2e 
in FY26 compared to 1,090.49 tCO2e in FY25, a near-zero net 
change achieved despite the commissioning of the 20,000 sq 
ft well-being precinct at Hyderabad SEZ, the activation of a 
4,000 sq ft collaboration space at Hyderabad TTC, and the 
addition of a second floor at our Bengaluru campus in FY25. 
Scope 3 emissions, now covering four categories, totalled 
3,458.07 tCO2e in FY26; the increase from FY25 reflects both 
the addition of Category 3 (upstream energy) as a new 
disclosure category and higher capital goods expenditure, 
with business travel emissions rising in step with the company’s 
geographic expansion into new international markets. Total 
water withdrawal moderated to 7,947.76 kL from 8,059.40 kL in 
FY25. E-waste of 12.97 MT accumulated across the network was 
disposed in full through a certified vendor across all locations. 
Our ESG performance is disclosed in accordance with SEBI 
BRSR Core requirements and is independently assured to 
reinforce transparency and accountability. The sections that 
follow describe our FY26 initiatives, organised across seven 
thematic areas: energy and climate, water conservation, waste 
management, occupational health and safety, green spaces 
and biodiversity, sustainable infrastructure and facilities, and 
employee well-being spaces. Strategic Approach to Natural Capital

Our Natural Capital Strategy
These principles translate into structured programmes across

Energy and Climate
Our energy footprint comprises thermal energy consumed 
through backup power systems and transportation assets, 
together with electricity required to operate our offices and 
workplace infrastructure. In FY26, total energy consumption 
was 7,070.12 GJ compared to 6,653.05 GJ in FY25, an 
increase of 6.3%. The increase was largely attributable to the 
commissioning of additional employee-focused infrastructure 
at our Hyderabad campuses, including new wellness, 
recreation, and collaboration spaces that expanded the 
operational footprint of the facilities. 
While these investments resulted in slightly higher electricity 
consumption, they were accompanied by continued 
improvements in energy management practices. Energy-
efficient lighting, occupancy-based controls, motion sensors, 
and renewable energy generation remained integral to our 
operations, helping moderate consumption growth while 
supporting an enhanced workplace experience. 
Energy intensity, measured in gigajoules (GJ) per crore of 
revenue, improved from 1.94 in FY24 to 1.65 in FY25 to 1.60 in 
FY26. This sustained improvement across three consecutive 
years indicates that revenue growth has continued to outpace 
energy consumption growth -- a pattern consistent with Tanla’s 
asset-light, software-led business model. Thermal energy 
consumption has declined by 46% since FY24, reflecting the 
near-complete elimination of diesel generator dependence 
at Hyderabad SEZ. The corresponding rise in electrical energy 
consumption reflects conscious expansion of employee-facing 
infrastructure, not underlying inefficiency. 
The Administration function continues to support the 
organization’s sustainability agenda through responsible 
resource management and green workplace initiatives. 
Our focus is on creating an efficient, environmentally 
conscious, and employee-friendly work environment. 
These efforts contribute to strengthening our Natural 
Capital commitments and long-term ESG objectives.Lokesh Penmetsa

Energy Consumption by Office (GJ)At campus level, the most significant energy story is the near-
complete elimination of thermal energy at Hyderabad SEZ, 
which fell from 1,543.96 GJ in FY24 to 11.45 GJ in FY26 following 
the decommissioning of diesel generators -- a 99% reduction 
in campus-level thermal energy. Both the Hyderabad TTC and 
SEZ together now account for the majority of total electrical 
consumption, a natural consequence of the well-being 
precinct and collaboration infrastructure commissioned during 
FY26. The Bengaluru campus recorded a material increase in 
electrical energy as the office space was expanded and fully 
operationalised during the year. Gurgaon ValueFirst remains 
the largest single contributor to thermal energy, reflecting 
continued generator dependency that will narrow as fleet and 
backup power transitions are completed.

LED Lighting and Smart Controls - Universal 
Transition Across All Campuses
Every office in our network operates on 100% LED lighting. 
The transition was completed during FY23 and FY24 and has 
been maintained without exception through FY26. Beyond the 
hardware transition, the way lighting is controlled varies by 
campus in ways that reflect each location’s physical layout 
and operating patterns. At our Hyderabad SEZ campus and 
one of our Gurgaon campuses, occupancy-triggered motion 
sensors have been active since FY24 and continued through 
FY26. Across our remaining campuses, lighting is managed 
through team distribution protocols: zones are activated as 
employees arrive and switched off progressively as teams 
leave, with a final shutdown when the last employee exits the 
premises. This approach eliminates overnight and weekend 
standby loss without dependence on centralised building 
management systems, placing accountability directly with 
the people who occupy the spaces.

in FY26, contributing 3.46 GJ to our overall energy mix. While

Secondary Power Source
The single most material energy transition of FY26 at the campus 
level was the elimination of diesel generator dependency at 
our Hyderabad SEZ campus. In FY24, the campus consumed 
39,991 litres of diesel for backup power, a volume that reflected 
single-phase supply constraints and the consequent reliance 
on generator sets during grid outages. A dual-phase power 
supply installed in FY25 provided a reliable primary backup, 
and by FY26 diesel consumption at the SEZ had reached zero. 
The change reduced Scope 1 emissions from this campus to 
near-zero and removed a recurring local air-quality impact 
from the campus precinct.
RECD-Compliant Diesel Generator
Where diesel backup remains a necessity, we have moved to 
the cleanest available compliance specification. In FY26, one of 
our Gurgaon campuses commissioned a new diesel generator 
fitted with a Retrofit Emission Control Device (RECD) certified 
by the Central Pollution Control Board. The RECD captures 
particulate matter at source before it can be dispersed 
through the stack. The legacy generator was decommissioned 
as part of the upgrade. This transition reflects the principle that 
where elimination of a polluting technology is not yet feasible, 
the obligation is to operate the cleanest available version of it.
GHG Emissions, Scope 1 and Scope 2
Direct emissions under Scope 1 originate from diesel consumed 
in generator sets and from petrol, diesel and CNG used in 
company-owned vehicles and employee shuttles. Indirect 
emissions under Scope 2 originate from grid electricity 
purchased at each location. Emission factors are drawn from 
the UK Government GHG Conversion Factors 2026. The India 
grid emission factor of 0.71 tCO2e per MWh for FY26 is applied 
in accordance with updated Central Electricity Authority 
guidance.

a systematic fleet renewal programme under which ageing, 
higher-emission vehicles were replaced with newer models 
designed to more stringent fuel efficiency and emission 
standards, reducing fuel consumption per kilometre across 
the employee transport fleet.
