GHG Emissions, Scope 3
In FY25, Tanla published its first Scope 3 GHG inventory 
covering three categories most material to our operations: 
capital goods (Category 2), business travel (Category 6), and 
employee commute (Category 7). Total Scope 3 emissions in 
FY25 were 985.93 tCO2e, a 47% reduction from 1,876 tCO2e in 
FY24.The year-on-year movement in total Scope 3 emissions requires 
careful contextualisation. The reduction from 1,876 tCO2e in 
FY24 to 985.93 tCO2e in FY25 reflected a sharp decline in capital 
expenditure rather than a structural improvement in value 
chain emissions. The increase to 3,458.07 tCO2e in FY26 reflects 
two distinct forces: first, the addition of Category 3 (upstream 
energy) as a new disclosure boundary, which contributes 550.91 
tCO2e not previously reported; and second, a substantial 
capital investment programme in servers, storage, networking 
equipment, and end-user devices required to support business 
growth and technology modernisation. Both factors represent 
transparency improvements, not operational deterioration.
Expanding Scope 3 Disclosure Boundaries
In FY26, Tanla expanded its Scope 3 disclosure boundary for 
the second consecutive year, adding Category 3 (fuel and 
energy-related activities not covered in Scope 1 and Scope 
2) to the existing three-category inventory of capital goods, 
business travel, and employee commute. This is a progressive 
approach to Scope 3 transparency in line with GHG 
Protocol Corporate Standard guidance and SEBI BRSR Core 
expectations. Category 3 captures the embedded emissions 
in the production and transmission of the fuels and electricity 
Tanla consumes including upstream extraction and processing 
of diesel and petrol, upstream electricity generation losses, 
and transmission and distribution losses associated with grid 
electricity procurement across all five states where Tanla 
operates. For FY27, 
The addition of Category 3 reflects our commitment to 
progressively deepening the transparency of our emissions 
disclosure in alignment with GHG Protocol Corporate Standard 
guidance and evolving SEBI BRSR Core expectations. Category 
3 emissions in FY26 were 550.91 tCO2e, comprising upstream 
fuel emissions of 20.88 tCO2e, upstream electricity emissions 
of 368.83 tCO2e, and transmission and distribution losses of 
161.20 tCO2e.

Capital goods dominate the FY26 Scope 3 inventory at 
51% of total emissions, reflecting the scale of technology 
infrastructure investment undertaken during the year. Business 
travel is the second largest contributor at 23%, driven by the 
international customer and partner engagement activity 
described above. Category 3 upstream energy accounts for 
16%, comprising the emissions embedded in the grid electricity 
and fuels that Tanla procures but that fall outside the Scope 
1 and 2 boundary. Employee commuting contributes 10%, the

one to have declined year-on-year. Collectively, these four 
categories now provide a materially more complete picture 
of Tanla’s value chain emissions footprint than the three-
category inventory published in FY25.
The expanded inventory means that year-on-year Scope 3 
comparisons should be interpreted with care: the increase 
in total Scope 3 emissions from 985.93 tCO2e in FY25 to 
3,458.07 tCO2e in FY26 reflects, in large part, the addition of 
a new disclosure category and a significantly larger capital 
expenditure programme in FY26, not simply an increase in 
operational emissions. Capital goods emissions rose from 
366.97 tCO2e in FY25 to 1,770.11 tCO2e in FY26, driven by 
substantial infrastructure investment in servers, storage, 
networking equipment, and end-user devices to support 
business growth and modernise our technology estate.
Business travel emissions increased from 221.95 tCO2e in FY25 
to 807.38 tCO2e in FY26, a 264% increase that reflects Tanla’s 
deliberate geographic expansion into new international 
markets. As Tanla extended its commercial reach into APAC, 
Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe during FY26, 
the company made a considered investment in in-person 
engagement with enterprise customers and telecom operator 
partners across these geographies. This increase in business 
travel emissions is a direct expression of the growth of the 
company’s GTM engine and customer success function -- and 
of the international customer relationships that have been 
established as a result. Air travel accounted for the majority 
of these emissions, consistent with the cross-regional nature 
of the engagements. As these geographies mature and 
customer relationships become established, travel intensity 
per relationship is expected to moderate. Employee commute 
emissions moderated from 397.01 tCO2e in FY25 to 329.67 
tCO2e in FY26, a 17% reduction achieved against a backdrop 
of stable or growing headcount, reflecting both a measurable shift toward two-wheelers and public transport modes, and 
awareness created in employees towards greener options. 
Note: The year-on-year increase in total Scope 3 emissions reflects 
both the addition of Category 3 (upstream energy) as a new disclosure 
category in FY26 and higher capital expenditure in FY26. Category 3 
was not disclosed in FY25.
LEED Gold and Green Data Centre 
Certifications
Our Hyderabad SEZ campus retained its LEED Gold certification 
through FY26. First achieved in FY24, the certification provides 
an independently verified benchmark across energy efficiency, 
water conservation, indoor environmental quality, and 
sustainable materials. The framework governs not only the 
building’s base performance but the design logic against 
which all facility upgrades are tested. Our green data 
centre certification, achieved in FY25, also remains in force. 
Virtualisation of IT infrastructure continues to reduce the 
computational hardware footprint and the energy draw that 
accompanies it.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26136Water Consumption by Office Facility, FY26
Hyderabad TTC registered the most significant domestic water 
reduction across the network, declining from 2,552 kL in FY24 to 
1,980 kL in FY26, a 22% reduction over two years, attributable 
to occupancy management and water-conserving fixture 
upgrades. Hyderabad SEZ domestic consumption has 
remained stable at 3,090 kL for two consecutive years 
despite the addition of the well-being precinct, reflecting the 
offsetting effect of the rainwater harvesting and STP recycling 
infrastructure at the campus. Chennai and Bengaluru both 
recorded modest increases, consistent with higher headcount 
and expanded operations at those locations. Mumbai, 
following the office relocation in FY24, returned to a higher 
consumption level in FY26 as occupancy increased. The 
Gurgaon ValueFirst campus has held domestic consumption 
flat at 120 kL for three consecutive years through rainwater 
harvesting, a notable achievement given the headcount and 
operational growth at that location.
Rainwater Harvesting with STP Integration
At our Hyderabad SEZ campus, rainwater collected on the 
building terrace is channelled into a Sewage Treatment Plant, 
where it is treated and recycled for washroom flushing and 
garden maintenance. The closed-loop arrangement means 
that a significant proportion of the campus’s utility water 
demand is met without drawing on the municipal supply, 
effectively achieving near-zero utility water wastage. Fresh 
municipal water is reserved for drinking and food preparation. 
The system operates within the requirements of the campus’s 
LEED Gold certification, which mandates water efficiency 
standards that go beyond regulatory compliance.
Rainwater Harvesting
Rainwater harvesting for utility use at one of our Gurgaon 
campuses, operational since FY25, allowed domestic water 
consumption to be held flat at 120 kL in FY26, matching the 
prior year’s level despite higher headcount and expanded 
operations. The system feeds general utility lines for non-
potable use, releasing fresh supply for drinking and food 
preparation. 
Zero Water Wastage
Five of our seven offices operate within tech parks and 
Special Economic Zones, where building infrastructure, water 
management systems, and facility standards are governed by the development’s overarching environmental protection 
framework. At these locations -- one of our two Hyderabad 
campuses, one of our Gurgaon campuses, and our Mumbai, 
Chennai, and Bengaluru offices -- zero water wastage is an 
embedded operating condition, supported by the building’s 
own systems including rainwater harvesting, sewage treatment 
plants, and metered supply. Our remaining Hyderabad and 
Gurgaon locations are standalone buildings where water 
infrastructure is independently managed. At both locations, 
we operate under controlled usage norms and careful fixture 
maintenance to minimise wastage, though the structural 
conditions for zero wastage that tech parks and SEZ buildings 
provide are not available. Across the network, total water 
consumption declined from 8,059.40 kL in FY25 to 7,947.76 kL in 
FY26, a reduction of 111.64 kL year-on-year.
Drinking Water Quality Upgrade
In FY26, drinking water provision at our Hyderabad and 
Mumbai campuses was transitioned from reverse osmosis 
(RO) dispensers to packaged Bisleri mineral water. The 
change addressed a specific and well-documented health 
consideration: RO purification, while effective at removing 
contaminants, also strips essential minerals -- including 
calcium, magnesium, and potassium -- that the body requires 
for long-term health. Mineral water consumption at Hyderabad 
TTC was 61.62 kL and at Hyderabad SEZ was 59.74 kL in FY26. 
Mineral water is also the standard at our Bengaluru campus. 
Our Gurgaon, Chennai, and Mumbai offices currently operate 
on RO systems, and the transition to packaged mineral water 
at these locations is planned for FY27.
Water Efficiency Infrastructure
Pressmatic taps and water-saving fixtures are standard across 
our office restrooms since FY24. Each tap delivers a metered, 
time-limited release and closes automatically, eliminating 
the cumulative wastage that conventional fixtures allow. 
These installations are incorporated into every refurbishment 
and renovation scope across the network as a baseline 
requirement.
Waste Management
Our waste management framework follows the Reduce-
Reuse-Recycle hierarchy and operates within the Central 
and State Pollution Control Board regulatory framework. 
Waste is tracked across non-hazardous, hazardous, and 
e-waste categories at each location and disposed of through 
authorised channels with appropriate documentation.
The Administration team made significant strides 
in enhancing workplace efficiency and employee 
experience throughout the year. Key initiatives 
included the modernization of office infrastructure, 
streamlining of vendor and facility management 
processes, improvement in workplace safety measures, 
optimization of travel and asset management systems, 
and the introduction of employee-friendly workplace 
enhancements. The team also successfully managed 
office expansion and renovation projects, reduced 
operational turnaround times, strengthened cost 
optimization efforts, and ensured seamless support for 
company-wide events and business operations. Through 
these initiatives, the Administration function continued 
to build a more efficient, collaborative, and employee-
centric workplace while driving operational excellence 
across the organization.Sabino Fernandes
Associate Director, 
Administration

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Cross-Location E-Waste Clearance Drive
The most significant waste management action of FY26 was a 
comprehensive e-waste clearance drive coordinated across 
all our major campuses. Form 6 certifications were obtained 
for each disposal lot under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 
providing full regulatory traceability from point of collection 
to point of recycling.
In total, 12.97 MT of electronic waste was disposed of during 
the year, covering decommissioned servers, racks, switches, 
cables, DG sets, UPS units, IT peripherals, and wiring 
assemblies. This was a deliberate strategic decision, not 
simply a housekeeping exercise. The e-waste disposal was a 
conscious choice to reduce accumulated technology debt, 
retire ageing infrastructure, and transition to newer-generation 
equipment with a significantly lower energy draw and carbon 
footprint per unit of compute. By decommissioning legacy 
hardware that consumed disproportionate power relative to 
its output and replacing it with modern infrastructure designed 
to higher energy efficiency standards, the exercise contributes 
directly to our longer-term Scope 2 reduction pathway. The 
drive reset the network to a near-zero e-waste accumulation 
position at year-end, with all disposed items fully traceable 
through certified documentation.
Waste Segregation
Waste segregation at source is practised across all our office 
locations. Designated bins for paper, cardboard, plastic, 
organic waste, and electronic items are placed at every waste 
generation point -- pantries, workstations, and common areas 
-- ensuring that waste is correctly sorted before it leaves the 
building. Wet waste from cafeterias is separated daily and dry 
recyclables are directed through their respective streams. The 
discipline is reinforced through visible signage at all disposal 
points and through inclusion in employee induction.
Paper Consumption Reduction 
Paper waste across the network stood at 1,666 kg in FY26, a 
marginal increase from 1,590 kg in FY25. The uptick reflects the 
partial-year nature of implementation -- print controls were 
introduced during FY26 rather than at its start -- alongside 
expanded office space and a higher average headcount 
across our campuses. With print controls now embedded 
across our Hyderabad campuses and rollout planned for the 
remaining network in FY27, the reduction in paper entering 
the waste stream is expected to be measurable in the next 
reporting cycle.
Food Waste Management
Food consumption across our campuses is managed through 
location-specific models, each designed to close the gap 
between food ordered and food consumed. At our Hyderabad 
campuses, Food Committees constituted in FY25 provide a 
structured daily feedback channel on quality, portion sizing, 
and consumption, with ordering anchored to four weeks of 
historical data and HR attendance inputs -- a mechanism that 
became fully embedded in FY26. At our Bengaluru, Gurgaon, 
and Chennai offices, food consumption is tracked against 
historical occupancy trends and feedback is managed directly 
by campus administration teams. At our Mumbai office, an 
individual in-person ordering model ensures that food is 
prepared only against confirmed orders, eliminating bulk 
preparation waste at source.
Hazardous Waste
Hazardous waste from our operations is limited to DG lube oil 
generated when generator sets are serviced. The volume is 
small in absolute terms and is disposed of through authorised 
channels under proper manifest documentation. In FY26, no 
hazardous DG lube oil waste was generated, as the elimination 
of diesel generator use at our Hyderabad SEZ campus reduced the overall generator servicing requirement across the network. 
The hazardous waste generation profile is expected to narrow 
further as generator dependency reduces.
Occupational Health and Safety
No workplace injuries or OHS-related incidents were recorded 
across all offices in FY26. This outcome reflects a sustained 
programme of drills, formal response structures, infrastructure 
upgrades, and contractual obligations that extend our safety 
standards to every person operating within our campuses.
Fire Drills, All Campuses
Fire evacuation drills are conducted on a half-yearly or annual 
cycle across all campuses based on the age of the facility. 
This cadence keeps protocols active in working memory and 
ensures that new employees encounter the procedure within six 
to twelve months. Each drill tests evacuation routes, assembly 
points, ERT response times, and the operational readiness 
of fire detection and suppression systems. A dedicated fire 
safety refresher training session was conducted in FY26 for all 
employees and facility staff, covering extinguisher handling, 
evacuation discipline, and the specific protocols relevant to 
each building’s layout. 
Fire System Upgrade
The fire safety infrastructure was upgraded at two of our 
campuses in FY26. The legacy detection and suppression 
system was decommissioned and disposed of through 
approved environmental channels. A new DG-connected 
fire suppression system was installed in its place, providing 
continuity of fire response capability even during power 
outages. The upgrade ensures that the campus operates 
with best-in-class life-safety infrastructure aligned to current 
regulatory standards.
Emergency Response Teams, Quick Response Teams, and 
Medical Preparedness
Emergency Response Teams and Quick Response Teams are 
formally constituted and operational across all seven of our 
offices, with named members, documented roles, and periodic 
training conducted at every location. In FY26, safety training 
programmes were conducted across the network, covering 
fire evacuation procedures, emergency response protocols, 
and first-aid preparedness. At our Hyderabad campuses, 
preparedness extends further to CPR training conducted by 
an in-house medical professional with more than 40 years 
of clinical experience. Sessions cover chest compression 
technique, rescue breathing, and the use of automated 
external defibrillators. The same medical professional is 
available on call during working hours and serves as the 
primary clinical resource for the dedicated medical room within 
the Hyderabad SEZ well-being precinct.
Health and Safety Standards Extended to Vendors
Out Employee Health and Safety Policy is published and 
maintained across the network. OHS obligations are written 
into contracts with all facility management vendors, covering 
housekeeping, security, and technical operations personnel. 
This ensures that safetystandards do not vary by employment 
relationship. Every person operating within our campuses, 
regardless of who employs them, is subject to the same 
baseline safety requirements that govern our own employees.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26138Green Spaces and Biodiversity
The biodiversity our campuses can support is necessarily 
modest, but it is actively cultivated. Across the network, we 
maintain indoor plants and landscaped exteriors, with a 
continuing focus on native and oxygen-generating species. 
The purpose is twofold: to support indoor air quality and 
employee well-being directly, and to ensure that our 
campuses contribute positively to their immediate ecological 
surroundings.
Indoor plants are maintained across all seven of our offices as 
a standard facility practice. Each campus maintains a curated 
selection of species chosen for their air quality and well-
being benefits, treating the office’s indoor ecology as a living 
system that requires active upkeep rather than a one-time 
installation. At all our campuses, this takes the form of a monthly 
replacement cycle -- plants that have completed their display 
cycle or show signs of stress are replaced with fresh specimens, 
ensuring a consistently healthy environment throughout the 
year. At our Hyderabad and Gurgaon campuses, oxygen-
generating species are deployed across all occupied floors, 
with new additions made in FY26 as part of building renovation 
and expansion programmes. Certain species maintained 
across our campuses are known to filter volatile organic 
compounds from indoor air and continue oxygen release 
through the night, providing a functional benefit to indoor air 
quality alongside the aesthetic contribution to the workspace.
Integrated Facility Management
In FY26, Tanla transitioned to an Integrated Facility 
Management model across its office network, consolidating 
what were previously fragmented, location-specific vendor 
arrangements into a unified operational framework. The model 
was first deployed at our Hyderabad SEZ, Hyderabad TTC, and 
Mumbai offices, covering approximately 40 personnel under a 
single integrated vendor relationship, and is being extended 
progressively to our remaining locations in FY27.
The consolidation delivers three concrete benefits. First, 
procurement volumes consolidated under a single purchase 
order have yielded meaningfully better unit costing, reducing 
the administrative overhead of managing multiple vendor 
contracts simultaneously. Second, environmental and safety 
standards -- covering waste segregation, water management, 
and energy operating procedures -- are now trained once, 
applied uniformly, and audited through a single accountability 
structure across all covered locations. Third, the management 
capacity previously consumed by coordinating multiple vendor 
relationships has been redirected to higher-value facility work, 
resulting in faster resolution of maintenance issues, more 
consistent service quality, and a facility environment that 
operates as a single coherent system.
Proactive Preventive Maintenance with BCP Integration 
Maintenance schedules at our campuses are structured as 
proactive, forward-planned programmes rather than reactive 
responses to equipment failure. Maintenance intervals are set 
ahead of expected wear thresholds, and programmes are 
integrated with our Business Continuity Plan, treating facility 
uptime -- including air-handling, water systems, and power 
infrastructure for in-house data centres -- as a direct input to 
operational continuity. Technology debt is explicitly addressed 
within the BCP framework, replacing infrastructure before 
expected failure intervals, reducing unplanned downtime, and 
extending the life of assets still within their optimal operating 
range. 
Employee Well-being Spaces and Recreation
Some of our largest infrastructure investments of FY26 were 
directed at employee well-being. A 20,000 sq ft well-being 
precinct came online at our Hyderabad SEZ campus, combining 
a full-service cafeteria, doctor’s consultation room, sports arena, indoor turf, table tennis, basketball, chess, carrom, and 
multiple collaboration zones under a single integrated design. 
A 4,000 sq ft space at our Hyderabad TTC campus, designed 
for collaboration and informal engagement, extends the same 
principle across both Hyderabad locations. At our Mumbai and 
Bengaluru campuses, recreational facilities are maintained 
at a scale appropriate to each office and remain consistently 
accessible through the working day. Across locations, the HR 
team has driven utilisation through structured programming, 
with Tanla Premier Leagues for table tennis, chess, and 
other indoor sports creating competitive, cross-functional 
engagement during the year. The same air purification, 
ventilation, and indoor environmental standards that govern 
the LEED Gold-certified SEZ facility apply throughout the 
precinct, reflecting our conviction that indoor environmental 
quality and employee well-being are not separate priorities 
but expressions of the same commitment.
Looking Ahead
Three priorities will define our natural capital work through 
FY27. 
1. Extension of the Integrated Facility Management model 
across all remaining offices in the network, bringing the 
environmental and operational standards now established 
at Hyderabad and Mumbai to every location we operate. 
2. Structured expansion of on-site renewable energy 
generation, informed by the operational experience 
accumulated from the Gurgaon solar system, targeting 
additional sites with suitable conditions for solar installation. 
3. Completion of full Integrated Report assurance across 
all environmental data for FY26, building on the assured 
disclosure obtained for FY25.
The broader trajectory we are working toward is clear. Scope 
1 emissions should remain on a downward path as diesel 
dependency continues to reduce across the network. Scope 
2 emissions should decouple from operational growth as 
the renewable share of our electricity mix increases. Scope 
3 disclosure will continue to expand: having added new 
categories in FY26, we are evaluating relevant Categories in 
1 and 11 for FY27, with the objective of progressively closing 
the gap between our reported inventory and a full value chain 
emissions picture. Water withdrawal should shift further toward 
recycled and harvested sources. Waste generation should 
compress through source reduction as our procurement, 
admin, and operational disciplines become progressively 
more embedded. These outcomes will arrive, as the changes 
of FY26 have arrived, through the steady, unglamorous work of 
holding environmental standards in every operational decision 
our facility teams make each day.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26140At Tanla, CSR is a deeply held commitment to the communities 
we serve, one that goes beyond supporting individuals to 
creating conditions in which entire families and communities 
can thrive. Every initiative Tanla Foundation undertakes, 
whether in education, health, or livelihoods, is designed with 
one question in mind: how could the communities benefit 
from this in the long-term? FY26 reflects that thinking in 
action. From building a health centre that serves ten villages, 
training youth for careers in data science, to acquiring land 
for a skill development institution, each initiative is a brick in a 
larger structure: self-sustaining communities that do not need 
external support to grow, but have the foundation to grow on 
their own.
This year, Tanla Foundation channelled a total CSR spent 
of INR 9.25 Crore across 9 distinct community-facing 
initiatives spanning education, primary healthcare, youth 
skilling, rural livelihoods, and cultural development. Every 
programme in this portfolio was preceded by a formal needs 
assessment or community-level consultation, ensuring that 
our investments respond to what communities actually need, 
rather than what is convenient to deliver. This is the principle 
we call ‘Empowerment by Design’, the conviction that lasting 
community transformation is best achieved not by arriving 
with solutions, but by listening first, designing collaboratively, 
and building local ownership into every intervention from the 
outset. 
The geography of our impact in FY26 is concentrated and 
intentional. Gangaram, located in Sathupally mandal, 
Khammam district, Telangana, identified by the Government 
of India as an aspirational district, listed in the MyMSME 
List of Aspirational Districts (Phase 1), is the anchor of Tanla 
Foundation’s community work. Here, children at the Sri 
Dasari Veera Reddy (SDVR) Government School are receiving 
structured academic support through PILLARS (Project for 
Improvement of Learning Levels through Academic and 
Other Support in Rural Schools), now in its fourth consecutive 
year. Residents of Gangaram and its neighbouring villages, 
including residents from bordering villages in Andhra Pradesh, 
are accessing free outpatient healthcare at the Tanla Rural 
Health Centre (RHC), a primary healthcare facility established 
by Tanla Foundation in the heart of the community. Covering 15 
villages, the RHC served 2,784 patients in its first 3 operational 
months, reaching 11% of the total catchment population. 
~12 acres of land has been acquired in Gangaram to anchor an 
Integrated Skill Development Centre, a permanent community institution that will serve 20,000 or more individuals from the 
surrounding 20-kilometre radius in the years ahead.
Building on its scholarship partnership with IIT Madras, now 
in its third year, Tanla Foundation’s reach extended further to 
the classrooms of IIIT Basar in Adilabad, where 100 forth year 
students received industry-aligned training in Data Science 
and Artificial Intelligence, 41 of whom have already 64 secured 
employment.
The Cyberabad Traffic Pulse initiative extended Tanla 
Foundation’s reach to the streets of Hyderabad, growing 
from 14,480 to 31,568 subscriber-citizens in a single year. 
Powered by Tanla’s own communications infrastructure 
across WhatsApp, Google RCS, and SMS, the initiative is a 
live demonstration of how an AI-Native Platform company can 
put its core capabilities directly in service of the public.
Tanla Foundation’s community engagement extended to 
the broader Sathupally Mandal through Sankranthi Utsavam 
2026, a five-day cultural and sports celebration that engaged 
850 participants from 20 villages. The event was designed 
from the ground up to be truly inclusive, government school 
students from Grade 1 through Grade 10 participated in 
age-appropriate sports and competitions ranging from 
poem recital, lemon and spoon, to kabaddi and kho kho 
competitions, while adults from across the mandal, both men 
and women, were encouraged to take part through volleyball, 
rangoli, and cultural activities. No age group was left out, and 
no one was a spectator by default. Sankranthi Utsavam 2026 
was a celebration of community in the fullest sense, every 
generation, every village, on the same ground, at the same 
time.
FY26 has been a year of concentrated, intentional spent. 
INR 9.25 Crore was directed to geographies where the 
development gap is widest, and over 35,683 lives were 
touched across communities that have historically had the 
least access to quality education, healthcare, and economic 
opportunity. 50% of those reached belong to marginalised 
groups, a figure that is not incidental, but a direct result of 
designing every programme around those who need it most. 
This is what purposeful CSR looks like: not spread thin across 
many causes, but rooted deeply in the communities where 
Tanla Foundation has chosen to show up, year after year, with 
long-term commitment.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Governing Social Capital
Good governance is the difference between a CSR programme 
and a CSR commitment. Our governance architecture for 
community investments is designed to ensure that every rupee 
spent is traceable to a community need, every outcome is 
measurable, and every decision, from strategic direction to 
field-level implementation, carries clear accountability. 
Oversight operates across three distinct tiers. The Board of 
Directors holds ultimate responsibility, ensuring that CSR 
strategy is aligned with the Company’s broader purpose and 
values. The CSR Committee, constituted under Section 135 
of the Companies Act, 2013 and chaired by an Independent 
Director, recommends the annual action plan, approves 
programme expenditure, reviews implementation progress, 
and monitors policy compliance. Tanla Foundation serves as 
the operational arm: identifying, designing, implementing, and 
evaluating all community-facing programmes on the ground. 
Together, these three bodies form a governance chain that 
runs from the boardroom to the beneficiary.
Five principles that guide every programmeIn FY26, this framework was put to its most significant test 
yet. With nine simultaneous programmes running across 
geographies, beneficiary groups, and development themes, 
the Foundation’s governance machinery was required to 
operate with the rigour of a structured institution, not the 
flexibility of a charitable initiative. Every programme in the 
FY26 portfolio was preceded by a formal needs assessment 
or a request from a credible implementing institution, ensuring 
that community voice, drove investment decisions. Site-level 
monitoring and independent assessments are embedded 
into each programme, with outcomes tracked against targets 
articulated at the point of programme approval.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26I. Education: Leaving No Learner Behind
Education is the foundation upon which Tanla Foundation’s 
social strategy is built. Despite India’s strides in school 
enrolment, learning quality in rural government schools remains 
a persistent challenge, compounded by socioeconomic 
barriers, language transitions, and limited access to digital 
learning tools. This year Tanla Foundation’s education 
portfolio encompassed three distinct programmes, each 
targeting a different stage of the education continuum, from 
primary schooling in rural Telangana to premier engineering 
institutions, together reaching 381 students.
PILLARS:  Project for Improvement of Learning Levels 
through Academic and Other Support in Rural Schools
INR 22,450
CSR Spent363 Students 
Beneficiaries
PILLARS is Tanla Foundation’s longest running and most deeply 
embedded educational initiative, now in its fourth consecutive 
year at SDVR ZP Secondary School, Gangaram, Telangana. 
Launched in August 2022, the programme operates on a 
foundational belief: that academic underperformance in rural 
government schools is not a reflection of student potential, 
but of systemic resource gaps that structured, sustained 
interventions can bridge. 
In FY26, the programme continued to support 363 students, 
with particular focus on identified at-risk students in Classes 
6 through 10. A rigorous baseline assessment conducted at 
programme commencement enabled the identification of 
students with the greatest academic need. Additional teaching 
resources were deployed to provide structured, curriculum-
aligned support in Mathematics, Science, and Social Studies 
during allocated school hours, ensuring the intervention is 
embedded within, not parallel to, the school day.Digital learning received significant reinforcement this year. 
Classroom televisions and Diksha-loaded tablets, aligned 
with the Telangana state-approved syllabus for Classes 6 
to 9, were installed and operationalised, creating an audio-
visual learning environment that makes abstract concepts 
tangible and engaging. Five dedicated Tanla Foundation 
staff members (three teaching and two non-teaching) operate 
on-site, facilitating both academic instruction and student 
welfare monitoring. 
The outcomes are visible and sustained. Students who 
previously missed school frequently are now regular attendees. 
Participation in extracurricular activities and inter-school 
sports has increased. Most significantly, the programme 
has begun to shift a cultural norm: girls in Gangaram village, 
inspired by the learning transformation of peers like Kola 
Krishnakumari (Class 7), are increasingly asserting their right 
to education and aspiring to higher academic attainment.
Over the last five years here in Gangaram, we at Tanla 
Foundation strengthened learning and wellbeing by 
focusing on core activities which included classroom 
teaching and remedial support, attendance and 
follow-up, digital lessons on the Dheeksha app, 
assessments, exam support, and school events. As 
trained educators, nothing makes us happier than 
teaching and nurturing young minds, especially 
students who lack family support, because we believe 
in enhancing lives through care, guidance, and quality 
instruction.
Tanla Foundation Teachers at SDVR 
Government school, Gangaram, Tanla Foundation

SDG Alignment:II. Healthcare: Bringing Primary Care to 
the Last Mile 
Rural Health Centre, Gangaram 
INR 17.84 Lakhs
CSR Spent2,784 Unique Patients  
Beneficiaries
 
Access to affordable, quality healthcare remains one of 
the starkest divides between rural and urban India. For the 
residents of Gangaram and its neighbouring villages, the cost 
of travel, the time away from work, and the uncertainty of care 
at distant facilities were significant deterrents to seeking timely 
medical attention. Tanla Foundation set out to change that by 
building a primary healthcare institution from the ground up. 
Understanding the Community Before Building the Solution 
Between September and December 2025, Tanla Foundation 
conducted a comprehensive door to door health situation 
assessment across Gangaram and six adjoining villages 
covering a population of 14149, to understand the community’s 
true relationship with healthcare, and the perception they 
carried of formal medical care.
The results presented by the assessment were that - across all 
seven villages, the Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) was 
the first point contact for all medical issues. Seasonal ailments 
and common infections were managed through home remedies 
as a default first response. The government Primary Health 
Centre was consistently bypassed, with residents expressing a 
desire for better quality of care, faster diagnostics, and a more 
respectful patient experience. Community leaders across the 
surveyed villages welcomed the idea of establishing the Rural 
Health Center (RHC) and committed to encouraging residents 
to use the facility, reflecting the genuine need and demand 
for quality and trustworthy primary healthcare in the region.
The assessment found that healthcare decisions within 
households were shared to varying degrees across villages, 
with many families making health-related choices together. 
This understanding shaped how the RHC communicates with 
and engages its patient community. What the assessment 
ultimately confirmed was that the community needed a 
healthcare facility it could rely on; Tanla RHC was built to be 
exactly that.

Building the Rural Health Centre 
The Tanla RHC was registered and operationalised in January 2026 with the Health Medical and Family Welfare Department, 
under the purview of the District Registering Authority, Khammam, Telangana. The clinical team comprises one full-time general 
physician registered with the Telangana State Medical Council, four qualified nurses, a dedicated data entry operator, and a 
pharmacist registered with the Telangana State Pharmacy Council. The Foundation holds a formal pharmacy licence issued 
by the Drugs Control Administration, Telangana. Every consultation is free. Every prescribed medicine is provided at no cost.
The Pharmacy 
The RHC pharmacy stocks medicines covering the most prevalent conditions identified in the assessment. The RHC distributes 
medicines worth INR 1.5-2 lakhs every month, including the medicines prescribed by doctors during tele-medicine consultation.
Who the RHC Serves
 
Of the 2,784 unique patients served, 55% were female and 45% were male. The largest cohort fell in the 45-64 age group at 40% 
of visits, with patients above 65 years accounting for 18%. The top four conditions treated were blood pressure & diabetes (22%), 
joint pains (47%), gastroenteritis (22%), and seasonal ailments (9%). 21% of patients were repeat visitors. Patients from bordering 
=== page 148 ===
147
#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26villages in Andhra Pradesh accounted for 4% of total visits, 
underscoring the RHC’s role as a regional healthcare anchor.
Patients schedule appointments via WhatsApp Business 
or phone prior to their visit. On arrival, they are registered 
using Aadhaar details into the Clinical Management System 
(CMS). Where patients do not have an Ayushman Bharat 
Health Account (ABHA), the RHC assists in generating one 
on-site. ABHA is a unique digital health identifier that gives 
patients a portable, lifelong health record accessible across 
hospitals and clinics anywhere in India, and enables access 
to government health schemes and insurance benefits linked 
to the Ayushman Bharat programme. Post registration, 
the clinical team examines the patient before the doctor 
prescribes the required medicines. The pharmacist dispenses 
medicines via an automated CMS alert and all records are 
maintained digitally. Patients are guided on their treatment 
plan and next steps before leaving the facility.  
Telemedicine: Connecting Villages to Specialists 
Launched in March 2026, the RHC’s telemedicine infrastructure 
connects patients to four specialist consultants: a 
Pulmonologist, an Orthopedic specialist, a Cardiologist, and 
an Endocrinologist.  Since its operationalization in March five 
tele-medicine sessions have been conducted and reaching 
46 patients with one session each being held for one hour. 
Regulatory compliances: 
The Tanla Rural Health Centre operates within a formal 
regulatory framework. The facility was registered under the 
Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 
2010 upon operationalisation in January 2026. The provisional 
registration, valid for one year, will be converted to permanent 
registration in the months ahead.

From Reactive to Preventive: The Road Ahead
As the Tanla RHC completes its first year of operations, the 
Foundation’s vision for community health extends beyond 
the clinic. The next phase of the programme will move from 
reactive care to preventive well-being. Plans are underway 
to develop a walking track in Gangaram village, build 
infrastructure to encourage sports and physical activity, and 
introduce structured well-being programmes for community 
members of all ages. These initiatives reflect the Foundation’s 
conviction that true healthcare is not just about treating 
illness, but about building communities where good health 
is a way of life.

Skill Training in Data Science and AI, IIIT Basar, Telangana
INR 54 Lakhs

BeneficiariesThe programme, which commenced in May 2025, was designed 
to bridge the well-documented gap between academic 
preparation and industry readiness in data science and 
artificial intelligence. Participants received intensive training 
in Data Science, Machine Learning, Natural Language 
Processing, communication skills, and entrepreneurial thinking 
through a combination of interactive workshops, mentoring 
sessions, and real-world project assignments. The curriculum 
was specifically designed to translate theoretical knowledge 
into applied problem-solving capability, the competency gap 
most frequently cited by technology employers.
The quality of the programme was independently validated 
through a student feedback audit conducted in October 2025. 
Of the 100 trained students, 98% rated trainer knowledge, 
theory-practice balance, and confidence in applying tools 
positively. The overall learning experience received a 94% 
positive rating. An industry exposure visit to T-Hub, Hyderabad,

between campus and the professional world.

lakhs per annum. Roles secured span Software Development, 
Full Stack Development, AI Engineering, Machine Learning, 
Data Science, and Backend Development, with recruiters 
including Tech Wave, Solve Systems Lab, PORUS, Edtex, and 
ForSys. An additional 35 students are in internship-to-full-
time conversion pathways, creating a longer runway toward 
permanent employment for students who are completing 
their final semester or awaiting degree confirmation.  
The programme has not only enhanced technical competency 
but has also measurably improved students’ confidence, 
professional communication, and entrepreneurial outlook. With 
35% of beneficiaries from marginalised groups, the initiative 
contributes meaningfully to equitable access to digital 
economy opportunities. For students from first-generation 
learner families in an aspirational district, a placement in a 
technology role is not just a first job. It is a generational shift.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26VI. Smart Cities and Digital Safety: 
Technology in Service of Society
Tanla’s identity as a an AI-Native Platform company gives it 
a distinctive opportunity: to deploy technology not just for 
commercial purposes, but as a public good. The Cyberabad 
Traffic Pulse initiative reflects this potential most clearly, 
leveraging Tanla’s core communications infrastructure to 
improve urban mobility and road safety at scale, at no cost to 
citizens or government.
Cyberabad Traffic Pulse, Cyberabad
INR 24 Lakhs  
CSR Spent 31,568 Citizens    
Beneficiaries
The Cyberabad Traffic Pulse (CTP) initiative, launched in 
January 2025 in collaboration with the Cyberabad Traffic 
Police and the Society for Cyberabad Security Council, 
completed its first full operational year in FY26, scaling from 
an initial 14,480 subscribers to over 31,568 citizens. This tenfold 
growth in a single year reflects the initiative’s relevance and 
the community’s appetite for real-time, actionable information 
about the roads they travel every day. 
Powered by Tanla’s communications infrastructure, including 
WhatsApp Business Platform, Google RCS, and SMS, the CTP 
service delivers real-time alerts on traffic congestion, VIP 
movements, major city events, accidents, and roadblocks 
directly to subscribers’ mobile devices. The service fills a 
critical information gap that existing navigation platforms do 
not address: the ability to communicate the reason for a delay 
and a realistic estimated resolution time, enabling commuters 
to make informed travel decisions before and during their 
journeys. 
The impact extends well beyond individual convenience. By 
reducing congestion-induced uncertainty, CTP improves 
the efficiency of emergency response, strengthens the 
collaborative relationship between law enforcement and 
the communities they serve, and sets a replicable standard for how technology companies can contribute to smart city 
development, not through one-time sponsorships, but through 
the sustained deployment of core competencies in service of 
the public good. 
In two years of operation, the initiative has delivered over 25 
million messages annually, with more than 31,000 subscribers 
relying on it as a primary source for road safety and civic 
information. It has been recognised at the highest levels of 
both CSR and academic impact assessment, affirming that 
the model works, and that it scales.

ESG Awards 2025 for its impact on road safety and urban mobility. The award 
acknowledges the initiative’s model of sustained, technology-enabled public 
service, delivered at no cost to citizens or government, and its demonstrated 
ability to scale rapidly while maintaining relevance and reliability for the 
communities it serves. 
The recognition affirms Tanla Foundation’s approach of deploying core 
organisational capabilities, in this case communications infrastructure, in 
direct service of a public need, rather than funding unrelated social projects 
as an afterthought to the business.
The Cyberabad Traffic Pulse initiative received Special Recognition at the IIT 
Madras Social Impact Awards 2026, marking the second consecutive year the 
initiative has been recognised by an independent academic institution for the 
quality and scalability of its social impact. 
This recognition is particularly significant in that it reflects evaluation by an 
academic body focused on the rigour and replicability of impact, not merely its 
scale. Having delivered over 25 million messages annually and grown to serve 
more than 31,000 regular subscribers, the initiative continues to demonstrate 
that public-private partnerships in digital infrastructure can generate durable, 
measurable community benefit.
Tanla was recognised for Best ESG Reporting and Transparency at the 
Global CSR and ESG Awards 2026, an acknowledgement of the Company’s 
sustained commitment to disclosure that goes beyond regulatory requirement. 
Tanla’s ESG reporting is built on GRI Standards 2021, the Integrated Reporting 
Framework, and SEBI BRSR Core, with environmental data independently third-
party assured and disclosures improving in scope and depth year on year. 
The recognition reflects specific choices Tanla has made beyond the mandate: 
an annually published Tax Transparency Report, CEO shareholder letters 
accompanying every quarterly result, and voluntary expansion of Scope 3 
emissions tracking in FY25. Each of these is a deliberate act of transparency, 
repeated consistently, and judged by this award to represent a standard of 
ESG disclosure that others in the sector can look to as a benchmark.
FY26 has been the year Tanla Foundation’s community work moved from a 
portfolio of programmes to the early architecture of permanent institutions. A 
Rural Health Centre that began as a need assessment is now a trusted point of 
care for fifteen villages. A land parcel acquired in Gangaram will, in the years 
ahead, become a skill development campus serving a twenty-kilometre radius. 
A traffic alert service built on Tanla’s own messaging infrastructure has grown 
into a civic utility relied upon by tens of thousands of citizens. What connects 
these is not scale alone, but a discipline of listening first: every programme 
this year was grounded in a formal need assessment or a credible institutional 
request, and every outcome was tracked against targets set before the first 
rupee was spent. 
FY27 will be a year of deepening rather than diversifying. The Rural Health 
Centre will add pathology laboratory and diagnostic services and move 
toward a permanent facility. PILLARS enters its fifth year with a wider cohort 
and stronger digital learning tools. The Integrated Skill Development Centre 
moves from acquired land to active construction. And the telemedicine network 
and CTP’s reach will all be tested against the same question that has guided 
Tanla Foundation since its founding: not how many lives were touched, but how 
durable that touch turns out to be. The Foundation’s ambition for FY27 is not

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Relationship Capital
Relationships That Compound
The nature of customer relationships at Tanla has deepened. 
What began as a commitment to operational reliability 
has grown, over more than a decade of partnerships, into 
something far more consequential: a shared stake in how 
enterprises, telcos, regulators, and law enforcement agencies 
communicate, engage, and protect their users in a trusted 
communications ecosystem. This is a distinction worth stating 
clearly. Tanla’s platforms serve the consumers of enterprises, 
delivered through telecom operators. But the measure of our 
success is ultimately felt one level further, by the subscribers, 
users, and consumers at the end of every communication, 
every transaction, every fraud alert, and every customer 
journey we power.
In FY26, two new telco partnerships one each in Indonesia 
and India, extended Wisley Ai’s protection to and additional 
200 million subscribers, bringing hundreds of millions of 
people under the safe umbrella of safer, more trusted digital 
communications. This is the compounding logic of telco 
relationships: every platform decision, every architecture 
investment, and every market entry anchored in a clear-eyed 
understanding of what our customers and their customers 
need, for the future.
Built for the Long Term
Tanla’s Customer Success function is not a support layer 
bolted onto a product. It is the operating mechanism through 
which every customer relationship is maintained, deepened, 
and made commercially durable. The function brings together 
professionals across technical account management, 
service delivery, and customer engagement, working in 
close coordination with the deployment team to ensure that 
customers receive continuous value from implementation 
through to long-term operation. In FY26, this commitment to 
structural depth was further reinforced with the appointment 
of a Chief Customer Officer for Tanla and the elevation of the 
Chief Customer Officer role at Karix, a signal that customer 
obsession is now a board-level priority, embedded in 
leadership accountability, not just service delivery practice.
Accountability Where it Matters
At Tanla, accountability is not a policy. It is a practice. When 
an issue arises, our teams own it completely, not just to log 
it, but to resolve it within TAT, to the full satisfaction of the 
customer. There is no deflection and no handoff for its own 
sake. Customer delight and customer feedback are the only 
measures our teams work towards.
The results are visible. CSAT has grown consistently over three 
years, from 42% in FY23 to 62% in FY24 to 76% in FY25, reaching 
84% in FY26 against a target of 80%. NPS has risen from 48 
in FY24 to 67 in FY26, against a target of 55, representing a 
22% outperformance against target. Both metrics reflect not a 
single intervention but a sustained, compounding investment 
in the quality of every customer interaction.One Goal, Every Function
Customer success at Tanla does not live inside a single 
function. It is a shared outcome that product, solutions, 
sales, engineering, and customer service teams are jointly 
accountable for delivering. Cross-functional alignment is at 
the centre. Sales and engineering teams engage on a regular 
cadence to resolve emerging customer challenges before 
they become escalations. Business Review Sessions serve 
as structured forums where customer voice directly shapes 
product and service priorities.
Dedicated Coverage for Enterprise Accounts
Tanla’s proactive engagement model rests on a deliberate 
design choice: do not wait for customers to surface problems. 
Our dual-layer support structure combines real-time service 
monitoring with structured account coverage, enabling us 
to identify and resolve issues before they affect business 
outcomes. In FY26, over 30 enterprise accounts receive 
dedicated Priority Support coverage, with response times as 
fast as 30 minutes for critical issues and assigned Single Points 
of Contact from both the Technical Account Management and 
Customer Success functions.
• Customer Success Managers are focused on solution-driven 
engagement, identifying opportunities to grow share-of-
wallet and co-create value for long-term value creation on 
both sides
• Technical Account Managers are assigned to key enterprise 
accounts as Single Points of Contact, responsible for 
resolving technical and operational issues with speed 
and precision, while supporting commercial growth and 
retention.

Every customer issue is an opportunity to demonstrate 
the quality of our service and to learn. Tanla’s complaint

closing tickets. It is a structured, multi-tiered system that 
ensures rapid acknowledgement, transparent communication, 
differentiated resolution based on issue severity, and 
systematic routing of complaint data back into product and 
process improvement.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26receipt through Freshdesk, our centralised ticketing platform. 
Every ticket generates an automatic acknowledgement with a 
unique reference number, creating a complete, time-stamped, 
and auditable record from open to close. This process is 
governed by a documented Standard Operating Procedure 
(SOP) that defines every step from initial receipt through to 
resolution, including acknowledgement timelines, escalation 
criteria, and communication standards. For critical Priority 1 
issues, the expected resolution timeline is communicated 
to the customer at the point of acknowledgement, ensuring 
complete transparency and allowing customers to plan 
around the resolution window. For all other issues, customers 
receive proactive updates as their tickets progress through the 
resolution pipeline. The SOP is version-controlled, available 
for audit, and forms the operational backbone of Tanla’s 
complaint management framework.
A Tiered Approach to Resolution
Tanla operates a tiered SLA framework that ensures the 
most business-critical issues receive accelerated attention 
while all accounts benefit from defined, transparent service 
commitments.
Of all tickets raised during the year, 99.97% were fully resolved 
within the financial year. A residual carryover of 0.03% of 
tickets, amounting to 58 open tickets as of 31 March 2026, were 
closed within the first week of April 2026. This near-complete 
resolution rate, combined with a formally documented SOP and 
system-enforced workflows through Freshdesk, demonstrates 
the operational resilience and governance maturity of Tanla’s 
complaint management infrastructure.
Customer Support Channels
Tanla provides customers with multiple, accessible channels 
through which they can raise issues, track resolution progress, 
and provide feedback. The breadth of these channels reflects 
our commitment to meeting customers where they are.
• Email and Online Ticketing via Freshdesk: Customers 
can raise issues directly through email, automatically 
logged as tickets. Every ticket generates an automatic 
acknowledgement with a reference number, creating a 
complete, auditable record of each interaction from open 
to close.
• Dedicated Phone and IVR Helpline: A dedicated helpline 
with an Interactive Voice Response system is available 
for all customers, providing immediate access to support. 
This channel is particularly valued for time-critical issues 
requiring verbal explanation and real-time guidance.
• In-Person and On-Site Support: For enterprise accounts with 
complex technical environments, Tanla provides on-site 
support capability, particularly relevant for deployment, 
integration, and escalation scenarios where physical 
presence adds resolution velocity.
• WhatsApp-Based Support: Tanla offers customer support 
via WhatsApp, enabling customers to raise and track issues 
through a channel they use daily. Especially effective for 
quick queries, status updates, and low-complexity service 
requests.
An AI-assisted virtual support layer is currently under 
development and is targeted for deployment in FY27, which 
will further extend Tanla’s resolution capacity for high-volume, 
low-complexity queries without compromising the quality of 
human-led engagement for complex issues.
Closing the Loop: From Feedback to Improvement
Complaint data at Tanla is not simply tracked for resolution 
metrics. It is systematically analysed and routed to 
engineering and product teams as a primary input for platform 
improvement. Delivery, latency, and failure-related issues represent the largest category of complaints, and this insight 
is directly feeding Tanla’s platform reliability roadmap. 
Account provisioning complexity and credit management 
workflows have similarly been identified as priority areas for 
process simplification, with dedicated improvement initiatives 
underway. It is this philosophy, of treating every complaint as a 
signal rather than a transaction, that underpins the sustained 
improvement in our satisfaction scores year over year.
Multi-Channel Support Infrastructure
Tanla maintains a multi-channel support infrastructure 
designed to ensure that customers can engage through 
their preferred mode of communication at any stage of a 
service interaction. In FY26, four distinct support channels 
are operational, with a fifth under active development for 
deployment in FY27.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26Responsible Supply Chain Management
Tanla’s commitment to innovation extends beyond product 
development to encompass how we source, collaborate, 
and deliver. Our supply chain is a strategic enabler, designed 
to be resilient, responsible, and forward-looking. Through 
close partnerships with suppliers and vendors, we co-create 
digital communication solutions that are agile, scalable, 
and aligned with our environmental and social responsibility 
goals. We view our supply chain as a critical driver of shared 
value, supporting business continuity while promoting ethical 
sourcing, sustainability, and inclusive growth.
Vendor Selection and Onboarding Standards
Our vendor ecosystem is shaped through a robust, criteria-
driven selection process. Every supplier we onboard is 
evaluated not only for cost-efficiency and scalability, but 
also for integrity, regulatory compliance, and sustainability 
alignment. We conduct competitive benchmarking by 
reviewing multiple bids, balancing pricing with long-term 
value, service quality, and ethical practices.
Each selected vendor is required to sign a declaration aligned 
with Tanla’s Supplier Code of Conduct, which outlines our 
expectations around responsible business conduct, labor 
standards, data security, and environmental compliance. 
Beyond onboarding, we conduct regular performance reviews 
and structured feedback loops to identify improvement 
opportunities and foster a culture of continuous collaboration 
and innovation.
In FY26, Tanla conducted awareness programmes on the 
Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) for 100% of its 
value chain partners, reinforcing data governance standards 
across the entire supplier ecosystem. This initiative reflects 
Tanla’s conviction that responsible data stewardship does 
not stop at our organizational boundary; it extends to every 
partner in our value chain.
Ethical Procurement Principles
Tanla’s responsible sourcing framework is built around six 
foundational commitments:Tanla’s six ethical procurement commitments
1. Integrity in Business Practices:  Strict compliance with 
all legal, regulatory, and ethical norms across every 
procurement interaction.
2. Fair and Inclusive Workplaces:  Zero tolerance for 
discrimination or exploitation, with full compliance 
with wage, benefit, and workplace safety regulations 
throughout the value chain.
3. Human Rights and Sustainability:  Prohibition of child or 
forced labor, and a preference for partners that actively 
demonstrate environmental and social responsibility.
4. Transparency and Governance:  A fully auditable 
Procure-to-Pay process with accurate, verifiable records 
enabling complete traceability.
5. Environmental Stewardship:  Proactive steps to reduce 
emissions, manage waste responsibly, and optimize 
resource usage across sourcing decisions.
6. Zero Tolerance for Corruption:  Strict disclosure norms on 
conflicts of interest, and robust checks against bribery 
and fraud.

Human Rights for Suppliers – Mitigation Strategies 
Our supplier ecosystem demonstrates a robust commitment to foundational human rights. We achieved 100% alignment across 
seven core areas, including adherence to local laws, fair working conditions, minimum wage compliance, respect for human 
rights, prevention of forced labour, provision of safe working conditions, and the maintenance of essential hygiene and maternity 
support standards. These figures confirm that our core ethical expectations are deeply integrated within the operations of our 
vendor partners. 
While these results are encouraging, they also identify specific areas for growth. In domains such as child labour policies and 
anti-discrimination frameworks, 12% of respondents reported uncertainty, highlighting a need for clearer policy communications. 
Furthermore, we identified a 25% gap in awareness regarding our SPEAKUP grievance redressal mechanism (speakup@tanl.
com), and similar levels of variance in environmental compliance, data protection, and professional development investments. 
Some variation in responses, including instances where certain policies are not yet applicable to smaller partners, highlights a 
need for greater engagement to ensure all vendors, regardless of scale, remain aligned with our comprehensive standards for 
a responsible and sustainable supply chain. These gaps represent opportunities where our partners benefit from additional 
guidance, training, and resources to fully align their internal systems with our comprehensive requirements.

procurement lifecycle, and ensure that every participant in the 
supply chain, from internal approvers to vendors, operates 
from a single, real-time view of every transaction.
The platform continues to deliver three foundational 
capabilities:
• Enhanced Accountability:  Clear ownership and auditability 
across the Procure-to-Pay cycle, with defined responsibility 
at each process stage.
• Process Transparency:  Real-time visibility into procurement 
and payment workflows for both Tanla teams and vendors, 
enabling faster and better-informed decision-making.
• Complete Audit Trail:  Detailed, immutable tracking of 
every transaction, providing the compliance and control 
infrastructure required to meet Tanla’s governance

Discussion 
and Analysis 
Global Economy 
The global economy grew at 3.2% in calendar year 2025 
(CY25), as estimated by the International Monetary 
Fund in its World Economic Outlook, broadly in line with 
previous calender year. While economic performance 
varied across regions, individual economies continued to 
be shaped by their distinct strengths, policy priorities, and 
market dynamics.
The most consequential development in CY25 was the 
announcement of a sweeping US tariff regime in April 2025, 
which triggered significant disruption to global trade flows 
and supply chains. Partial rollbacks and interim bilateral 
trade agreements followed in subsequent months, but the 
episode durably altered supply chain strategies across 
industries and geographies, accelerating diversification 
away from concentrated manufacturing bases. Against 
this backdrop, regional economies responded differently. 
The United States remained the most resilient developed 
economy, with strong labour markets and domestic 
consumption providing a stable foundation. Europe 
continued to face structural headwinds in the form of 
subdued industrial output, elevated energy costs, and fiscal consolidation requirements that kept growth 
below potential. China grew below its recent historical 
rates, weighed down by a prolonged property sector 
correction and softening export momentum in the face 
of tariff headwinds.
 
Emerging markets bore a disproportionate share of the 
impact from the US tariff regime. The effective US tariff 
rate on emerging market exports surged to nearly 20% 
through CY25, compared to approximately 4% prior to the 
current administration’s trade policy reset. Economies with 
deep integration into global goods manufacturing and 
export-led growth models faced the sharpest headwinds, 
with the IMF revising its emerging market and developing 
economy growth projection downward by 0.5 percentage 
points to 4.5% for CY25. 
CY25 was, in summary, a year of divergence. Economies 
and regions that entered the year with strong 
fundamentals demonstrated resilience. Those that were 
more exposed to trade disruptions and external shocks 
faced meaningful pressure. The global growth story of 
CY25 was not one of uniform expansion but of varying 
capacity to absorb and adapt to a rapidly shifting 
external environment.
=== page 164 ===

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26
Indian Economy 
India retained its position as the world’s fastest-growing major 
economy in FY26, with the GDP growth estimated at 7.7%, 
up from 6.5% in FY25. This performance, achieved against a 
challenging global backdrop, reflected the fundamental 
strength of India’s domestically driven growth model. Growth 
was broad-based across sectors. The services sector remained 
the primary engine, with financial services, trade, transport, 
and communication recording strong expansion through the 
year.
Manufacturing activity sustained momentum supported by 
Production Linked Incentive schemes, while government 
investment in infrastructure continued to underpin construction 
activity. The RBI reduced the repo rate three times through 
the year by a cumulative 100 basis points, bringing it to 5.25% 
as at March 31, 2026, supporting credit growth, household 
consumption, and business investment activity. Fiscal policy 
complemented monetary easing. The government maintained 
its capital expenditure programme while implementing income 
tax relief and GST rationalisation measures, providing direct 
support to consumer spending. 
India’s fiscal deficit continued on a consolidation path through 
the year. India’s export sector faced headwinds from the US 
tariff regime, with tariffs on Indian goods reaching up to 50% 
before an interim bilateral agreement brought the effective 
rate down to approximately 18%. 
India’s overall growth, however, remained largely insulated 
given the economy’s predominantly domestic demand 
orientation. The outbreak of conflict in West Asia in late 
February 2026, and the resulting disruption to global energy 
markets, introduced fresh uncertainty into India’s near-term 
inflation outlook given the country’s significant dependence 
on imported crude oil and natural gas.
Looking ahead, the Economic Survey projects India’s real GDP 
growth at 6.8-7.2% for FY27, supported by ongoing structural 
reforms, continued infrastructure investment, and a favourable 
demographic dividendIndustry Overview
The global CPaaS market is projected to reach USD 27.4 billion 
by 2029 (Gartner). India’s CPaaS market is estimated ~ at INR 
14,500 Cr (USD 1.7 billion), growing at 5-7% annually, with OTT 
channels now contributing approximately 50% of the mix. 
WhatsApp remains the fastest-growing channel, reflecting 
a clear shift by enterprises towards rich media, personalised 
engagement, and two-way communication.
The evolution of digital communication is now entering a 
new phase. What began as a shift toward multichannel 
engagement has progressed into AI-native, outcome-driven 
experiences, where enterprises increasingly recognise that 
their competitive differentiation lies in delivering seamless, 
personalised, and secure digital journeys at scale. 
User expectations have moved in the same direction, 
with real-time engagement, relevance, and privacy-first 
interactions now becoming baseline requirements rather than 
differentiators. These shifts are playing out against a more 
complex operating backdrop, where enterprises must balance 
growth ambitions with regulatory compliance, cost discipline, 
and the pressure to do more with less. 
Trust has also emerged as a critical dimension of this evolution, 
as rising instances of spam and fraud make it imperative for 
enterprises to ensure that every interaction is secure and 
verifiable.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26164Growth Drivers 
Demand is being reshaped by a structural shift in digital engagement, from enabling communication to delivering intelligent, 
trusted, and outcome-driven interactions at scale.
Opportunities 
Demand for digital communication continues to grow. Non-discretionary usage, led by BFSI, government, and other regulated 
sectors, is rising with the scale of India’s digital economy, with banking alerts, UPI notifications, and OTP volumes increasing 
alongside transaction growth. At the same time, discretionary spend in retail and e-commerce remains strong, with enterprises 
investing across the full customer lifecycle from acquisition and conversion through engagement and retention and increasingly 
directing budgets toward AI-led solutions that deliver measurable returns. OTT channels are opening new use cases for small 
and mid-sized businesses, further broadening the opportunity across the ecosystem.
 
For enterprises today, the question is not the choice of channel but how to reach the right customer, on the channel 
they prefer, with the right message at the right moment. Digital communication has evolved across the customer 
lifecycle, with different functions driving distinct outcomes — marketing teams enabling acquisition and engagement 
through conversational experiences, operations teams powering trusted transactional communication, and customer 
experience teams strengthening retention through personalised interactions. As OTT and SMS continue to play 
complementary roles in enterprise communication, the opportunity continues to expand with every new business use case.  
Regulatory focus on data security & privacy is intensifying, and market practices are evolving toward more 
secure, transparent, and consumer-centric models. This is creating greenfield opportunities in trusted 
communication that are largely new and still forming. With deep domain expertise in this space, we are well 
placed to build platforms that address these emerging needs as the ecosystem shifts toward higher standards.  
Across each of these dimensions, the opportunity is not just to participate in market growth but to shape how trusted, intelligent 
digital communication is built and delivered at scale.AI-Powered Customer

Digital communication today operates within a complex ecosystem of players — enterprises seeking to engage customers 
intelligently, users expecting relevant and trusted interactions, telcos that are both partners and enablers of communication 
infrastructure, and regulators mandating accountability, consent, and data privacy across the value chain. Sitting at the centre 
of this ecosystem, we play a role across every stage of the digital interaction value chain — from authentication and acquisition, 
through engagement and customer experience, to protection and retention.
The business operates through two segments. The Digital Platforms segment addresses the trust layer in digital communications, 
building AI-native solutions that protect users from spam, scams, and fraudulent interactions while enabling telcos and 
enterprises to operate in a secure and compliant environment.
The Enterprise Communications segment addresses the engagement layer, enabling enterprises to connect with 
users intelligently across channels, with a focus on delivering contextual, outcome-driven interactions at scale.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26168Revenues: 
Revenues are generated from our Digital Platforms and Enterprise Communications business. Digital Platforms revenues 
are recognized based on a revenue-sharing model, wherein earnings are determined as a percentage of the value of 
transactions processed through mobile carrier networks and other suppliers, at a price agreed as per the contract. In 
addition, revenues are also generated through usage-based models, including per-user billing and pay-per-use models.  
Enterprise Communications revenues are recognized based on the volume of transactions processed through our platforms, at 
a predefined fixed rate per transaction, as specified in customer contracts and fixed-price contracts.

wallet share.

Depreciation and Amortisation
Fixed assets, including IT assets, are depreciated over their estimated useful lives using the straight-line method. Intangible 
assets, recognised at the time of acquisition based on the purchase price allocation methodology, are amortised over their 
estimated useful lives using the straight-line method. The right-of-use asset, representing leased assets such as office premises, 
is depreciated over its useful life.
Depreciation and amortisation increased by 24.5% YoY to INR 122 Cr in FY26. The increase was primarily driven by amortisation 
of platforms that went live during the year, including Wisely.ai, and infrastructure upgrades to support platform operations.

The movement in retained earnings reflects a profit of INR 509 Cr generated during the year, offset by a dividend payment of 
INR 160 Cr to shareholders
Lease Liabilities
As per Ind-AS 116 on lease accounting, leased assets recognition as assets and liabilities is mandated in the lessee’s financial 
records. Accordingly, the asset and liability associated with leased office premises of the group companies have been determined 
and presented within non-current and current assets/liabilities. This classification pertains to values anticipated to occur after 
one year and within one year, respectively.
Long-Term Provisions 
Provisions represent liabilities accrued for leave encashment ( INR 4 Cr) and gratuity ( INR 17 Cr) payable to employees on 
retirement, resignation, or superannuation, quantified and charged to expenses at the end of reporting period. 
Gratuity liability is managed through a policy held with Life Insurance Corporation of India, to cover the liability as and when the 
claim arise. Leave encashment represents the accrued liability in accordance with our leave policy, which becomes payable 
to employees upon retirement, resignation, or superannuation. Both gratuity and leave encashment are accrued based on 
independent actuarial valuation reports.
Other non-current financial liabilities
Other non-current liabilities consist of security deposits received from customers.
Trade Payables
Trade payables primarily comprise amounts payable for cost of services (to mobile carriers) and other suppliers. As of March 31, 
2026, trade payables were INR 679 Cr, compared to INR 575 Cr as of March 31, 2025.

#TanlaIntegratedReportFY26174Other Current Financial Liabilities 
Other current financial liabilities consist of cost of services not yet billed to the company, payable to capital creditors, unclaimed 
dividend, amount payable towards corporate social responsibility expenditure and other financial liabilities.
An amount of INR 1 Cr is held within the unclaimed dividend account, representing unpaid dividends to shareholders over the 
years due to various reasons.
We have instituted appropriate oversight mechanisms through its registrar and secretarial team to manage this liability. In 
accordance with regulatory requirements, any unclaimed dividend remaining unpaid for seven years from the date of declaration 
is transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) maintained by the central government.

Other current liabilities consist of statutory liabilities, payable towards GST and TDS. These liabilities are settled with government

Accrued income represents revenue that has been accrued but not yet billed at the end of each month. This is a common industry 
practice where invoicing occurs in the following month after reconciliation. Accrued income for FY26 is at 11% of revenue.

Liquidity Management
The primary source of our cash, cash equivalents, and current investments is the funds generated from our operational activities. 
Over the years, these funds have been prudently utilised to support core business operations, drive capital expenditure in line 
with our growth strategy, and return value to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. As at 31 March 2026, our 
cash, cash equivalents, and current investments including fixed deposits and liquid funds were predominantly held in Indian 
Rupees and U.S. Dollars. In line with our treasury policy, we invest only in instruments rated AAA or equivalent. We are a debt-
